title: How lemonflow built real-time agents for EV charging using Gemma and TPUs
raw_text: Welcome back to The Blueprint, a regular feature where we highlight how Google Cloud customers are tackling unique and common challenges across industries using the latest AI and cloud technologies. We hope to inspire others looking to innovate in their work. As the electric vehicle revolution gains steam in Europe, every charging session is a moment of truth, for the driver and for the transition itself. At lemonflow , we build AI agents purpose-built for EV charging: support agents for drivers and monitoring agents for charging networks. Our support agents answer drivers around the clock in more than 90 languages, and today they help an EV driver every 90 seconds. The Challenge Before we founded lemonflow, we worked closely with leading mobility players across Europe and saw first-hand how often charging goes wrong: Between 15% and 25% of EV charging attempts in Europe end in failure. Across Europe’s rapidly expanding EV market, where battery-electric car sales grew 30% in 2025 and thousands of charge point operators run public chargers, drivers who encountered stalled charging points were often left stranded or stuck in slow call center queues. We set out to change that hands-on: to bring the cutting edge of AI to EV charging, and to build the world’s best conversational AI for distributed hardware, an automated platform that resolves real-time charging issues via phone, chat, email, and WhatsApp. However, handling live voice support created several technical requirements: Strict latency thresholds: Frustrated drivers want immediate assistance. Our testing confirmed that serving latencies above 800 milliseconds risk conversational barge-ins, causing drivers to interrupt the agent and break the interaction flow. Managed API bottlenecks: Initially relying on managed LLM APIs, we faced latency deviations during peak hours (spiking from 1.0–1.2 seconds to over 1.7 seconds) and experienced HTTP 429 rate-limit errors when global usage peaked. Compute-intensive conversations: Every agent works from one comprehensive prompt, paired with dynamic tool calls that read and act on live charger data. This design creates intense bursts of compute demand during calls, making throughput on shared, managed capacity difficult to guarantee under peak loads. Highly fragmented ecosystem: We needed a standardized conversational engine capable of bridging around 30 distinct Charge Point Management Systems (CPMS), the backends operators use to run their chargers, each with its own APIs, data models and quirks. Hundreds of tailored agents: No two operators run support the same way. Each has its own tariffs, payment methods, escalation paths and hours for human backup, and most run several agents, for example one per country, brand or hotline, with behavior that can change by time of day. Each agent’s prompt is unique and must be served at full speed and improved without breaking any of the others. To deliver ultra-low-latency voice interactions and guaranteed serving capacity, we needed direct control over our model hosting environment. The Solution We wanted every driver to get best-in-class support that feels effortless, almost magical: no queue, no menu, just a short conversation that ends with the car charging. Picture a driver on a long cross-border trip, pulling into a motorway service station at 11 p.m. She plugs in, but the charger won’t start: the previous session never closed properly. She calls the number on the charger and is answered in her own language. Within seconds, our agent spots the stuck session in the charger’s logs, restarts the charger remotely and stays on the line until power is flowing. To get there, we had to solve our latency bottlenecks and secure dedicated compute capacity. We migrated from managed APIs to self-hosting the open Gemma 4 model on Google Cloud TPU v6e hardware in the EU. Like many startups using Gemma , the compatibility of these open models with Gemini allowed us to transition our existing prompt infrastructure with minimal modification. Moving to self-hosted TPUs unlocked the more complete architectural control our engineering team required to establish a deterministic core layer that handles EV-specific guardrails, guards against prompt injections, and standardizes previously fragmented backend protocols into our internal format before ever reaching the LLM. Control had a second payoff: because the model and serving stack change only when we change them, every test result stays meaningful. That stability laid the foundation for Agent Coach, our background coaching engine for AI agents, described below. We then developed an intelligent routing gateway to prioritize workloads according to operational urgency, serving live voice calls first, followed by web chats, and deferring automated re-simulations to low-traffic periods. Custom optimizations to the open-source vLLM serving engine and memory tiering between the TPU and host memory let a single TPU slice keep many more operator agents ready for instant answers, without recalculating their context. We also implemented automated fallback routing to self-hosted GPUs and Gemini Enterprise endpoints. Thanks to TPU reliability, Gemma answers more than 99.9% of all live conversation turns, and these fallbacks serve primarily as deployment buffers during system updates. Primary or fallback, every request is served from secure EU compute. The Architecture The Outcome For the e-mobility companies we work with, and for their drivers, the result is support that simply works: our agents typically answer every call, handle more than 80% of conversations end to end without a human handover, and earn 95% driver satisfaction. Behind the scenes, self-hosting Gemma on Google Cloud TPUs transformed our performance: Rapid deployment cycles: Prompt update and test cycle times dropped from 2–3 hours to about 10 minutes, a more than tenfold faster improvement loop. Sub-second serving latency: We lowered our P50 latency to around 350 milliseconds and our P90 latency to around 600 milliseconds. That is roughly three times faster than our managed-API baseline and fast enough to sharply reduce customer barge-ins. Zero throttling and flat latency: Dedicated TPU infrastructure eliminated HTTP 429 rate-limit errors, and latency stays flat through peak afternoon call traffic. Testing without limits: On dedicated capacity, every TPU cycle that live conversations don’t need becomes testing capacity, so our team can experiment and validate at will. Built for scale: Today, our agents support more than 40 charging networks in 17 countries, covering more than 250,000 charge points, around the clock. And this is just the beginning: the same platform is ready to take on many more networks and markets. With additional compute capacity, we introduced Agent Coach , a background engine that provides agents with relevant context during live calls and turns real conversations into permanent test cases, so every call makes the next one better. We also added nightly automated regression testing across thousands of fixed conversational scenarios. Looking ahead, we are preparing to move to Ironwood, Google’s seventh-generation TPU, as soon as it is available in our EU region. With six times the high-bandwidth memory per chip, Ironwood will multiply the number of operator agents a single TPU can keep ready in memory for instant answers. Ultimately, our goal is that no driver is ever left stranded at a charger. They get an instant, expert answer in their own language, the charger is rebooted remotely if necessary, and our AI monitoring agents catch the next fault before another driver ever notices. Open models on dedicated Cloud TPUs give us the speed and control to make that the standard across Europe. The Details Our platform runs two kinds of AI agents: support agents that talk to drivers in real time, served by Gemma on Cloud TPUs for minimal latency, and monitoring agents that analyze conversations and charger logs in the background on Gemini, so operators can fix faults before the next driver is affected. To keep its core platform consistent across many kinds of e-mobility companies, from charge point operators (CPOs) and e-mobility service providers (eMSPs) to charger manufacturers, lemonflow built a translation layer that converts varied CPMS interfaces into a standardized format. When a driver calls the support line posted on a charger, the call reaches our Conversational Engine through the operator’s own hotline. The engine then pulls the charger’s live status and Open Charge Point Protocol (OCPP) logs, the messages chargers exchange with their backend, from the operator’s CPMS in real time. Because charging stations often lack digital displays, drivers are frequently unaware of underlying issues like pending mobile 3D-Secure payment authorizations, session timeouts, charging cards not enabled for roaming, power reduced by local load management, or a car that ended the session at its own charge limit. Our engine feeds structured log summaries directly into Gemma on TPU to inform interactions with drivers. Direct model control allows us to stream token output selectively. Partial text tokens stream instantly to our Text-to-Speech (TTS) engine, while structured tool-call tokens stream asynchronously to backend systems to execute real-world actions, such as remotely restarting chargers, unlocking stuck cables, stopping sessions that failed to end, sending drivers details via SMS or email, or notifying service technicians. Deterministic security controls screen inputs before they reach the TPU-hosted LLM, blocking malicious prompts. This architecture is designed with European critical-infrastructure requirements in mind, and it still keeps conversations snappy, with a typical response starting in around 350 milliseconds. In the end, all of this should stay invisible to the driver: they just get a fast answer and a charger that works. We’re proud to work with Google Cloud to make that the norm and help EV adoption keep growing.

title: Don’t just prompt AI — architect it: Introducing the Professional Agentic Architect Certification
raw_text: It just got easier to prove your expertise in building production-ready agents. Today, Google Cloud is introducing the Professional Agentic Architect certification as the latest milestone in our Gemini Agent Ready (GEAR) initiative. Nearly one million developers are using GEAR to skill up on agents, but what makes this particular certification so special is its adoption within Google’s walls. Over the past four months, Google Cloud has trained thousands of forward deployed engineers and strategic partners on our own advanced curriculum. Originally built as an internal training initiative, we are now opening it up to the entire developer community and partner ecosystem through this new certification. As the VP who manages our forward-deployed engineers here at Google Cloud (Ravi) and the managing director of Google Cloud learning (Gary), we’ve seen just how effective this program has been inside Google at helping our teams rethink the way they build, deploy, and use AI in everyday in almost every way. We’re equally about what this new certification can bring to everyone — developers, engineers, and anyone else ready to demonstrate their agentic leadership. New Google Cloud Agentic Architect Certification A new hybrid format to validate your real-world skills This is not a traditional multiple choice exam. Google has introduced a new hybrid format that requires you to prove both conceptual know-how and hands-on execution. Part 1 (The multiple choice proctored exam): Evaluates your system design choices, architectural standards, cost optimization, and security governance. Part 2 (Hands-on labs on Google Skills): Puts you in an active cloud environment to build, test, and debug live agentic workflows. Why earning this certification can help advance your career As enterprises look to find top AI talent, this certification immediately signals that you have the advanced skills necessary to design secure, governed, and high-performance multi-agent systems. Our research with Ipsos on AI skill building shows that certifications drive more recruiter outreach: 82% of learners using Google Skills say that mentioning Google Cloud certifications on their resume drives more recruiter responses . And it’s not just about getting the call — it’s about being able to answer it. That same research showed that 90% of cloud professionals say credentials like Google Cloud certifications give them the verified know-how needed to fill in-demand roles. What’s covered on the exam The certification validates your proficiency across five key domains: Build agents using low-code tools (democratizing rapid agent prototyping). Use coding agents for application development (supercharging your coding productivity). Develop custom agents on the Gemini platform with open source frameworks. Evaluate and deploy agentic workflows (monitoring, optimizing, and ensuring performance). Secure and govern agentic workflows (protecting sensitive enterprise data and ensuring model safety). Battle-tested by thousands of Google Cloud engineers and partners — now available to you Enterprise demand for agentic workloads has skyrocketed. title: Inside the Gemini factory: Accelerating partner solutions
raw_text: With the new unified Gemini experience, enterprises can bring third-party partner capabilities directly in Gemini through standardized connectors (spanning Model Context Protocol (MCP), Agent-to-Agent (A2A) runtimes, and REST APIs), alongside emerging declarative skills and plugins. For independent software vendors (ISVs), this unified architecture unlocks a powerful opportunity to embed domain-specialized intelligence, regulated workflows, and live systems of record directly into enterprises' daily workflows. Yet turning a compelling use case into an enterprise-ready integration often stalls in engineering friction, from choosing the right extensibility primitive and wiring authentication to orchestrating multi-step tool execution and rendering inline interactive experiences. To eliminate these bottlenecks, Google Cloud launched the Gemini factory—an intensive co-innovation initiative designed to help enterprise software partners go from a blank whiteboard to agentic solutions listed on Google Cloud Marketplace in record time. Through hands-on workshops in global technology hubs—including San Francisco, New York City, Sunnyvale, London, Paris, Tel Aviv, and Tokyo—Google Cloud specialists work side-by-side with partner teams to ideate, architect, and build the next generation of enterprise AI solutions with Gemini. Specifically, the Gemini factory helps partners: Choose the right agentic architecture across MCP connectors, skills, plugins, and autonomous agents. Go from an initial use case to a production integration in days rather than months. Accelerate customer activation with funding incentives and go-to-market (GTM) support. Let’s dive in and see how we make all of that a reality. Choosing the right architecture: agents, MCPs, skills, and plugins In previous iterations of enterprise AI, third-party integrations often operated as isolated top-level agents, forcing employees to leave their workflow. When software providers arrive at the Gemini factory, they evaluate how their capabilities plug into Gemini across four complementary architectural primitives rather than competing extremes: Model Context Protocol (MCP) connectors: The foundational data and tool pipe for exposing external APIs, search, and CRUD operations to Gemini as callable tools registered in Agent Registry in Gemini platform. Declarative Skills ( .md ): Open Markdown configurations stored in Skills Registry that equip Gemini with domain-specific instructions, operational guardrails, and repeatable multi-step workflows across connectors. Plugins: The composite packaging and governance primitive in Gemini and Google Cloud Marketplace that bundles one or more Connectors and Skills into a single turnkey solution for IT administrators to govern and Gemini users to invoke. AI agents (A2A): For enterprise ISVs whose value lies in proprietary algorithms, regulated workflows, or strict compliance rules, standalone A2A agents run in an isolated partner environment while plugging into Gemini as callable connectors—keeping intellectual property protected, guaranteeing deterministic execution sequences, and maintaining tamper-proof audit trails. Rather than forcing developers into a single mold, Gemini unifies all four primitives into a coherent enterprise fabric—passing shared session context into partner connectors and chaining outputs across the enterprise ecosystem. Technical velocity: From use case to production Once the right architectural pattern is defined, the Gemini factory compresses months of integration work into a streamlined, AI-assisted engineering pipeline that brings partner development teams and Google Cloud experts together side-by-side. Accelerated Partner Development Pipeline This execution velocity is powered by three core capabilities in Gemini platform: Antigravity & AI-assisted builder workflows: Rather than writing boilerplate from scratch, developers build and govern solutions in Antigravity, an AI-first development environment. Using pre-built Rapid Agent Development (RAD) skills and AI-assisted workflows, partner teams rapidly translate use-case specifications into working architectures, scaffold remote MCP connectors or agent runtimes, author declarative .md skills, and run automated pre-ingestion validation harnesses. Flexible backend primitives (MCP, skills, plugins, and ADK): For most integrations, teams expose platform APIs via a hosting-agnostic Remote MCP Connector (on Cloud Run or their existing cloud) and layer on declarative Skills ( .md ) bundled into a turnkey Plugin . When a use case requires closed-IP models or strict deterministic execution, partners use the Google Agent Development Kit (ADK) and the A2A protocol to expose their runtime as a callable connector in Agent Registry. Inline adaptive experiences (native MCP apps): Instead of redirecting users to fragmented external portals or maintaining complex custom UIs, Gemini keeps users in the flow of work. Through native MCP apps and guided inline components, partner integrations dynamically stream rich, context-aware visual canvases directly in Gemini while chaining outputs across Google Workspace and other enterprise connectors. From working prototype to marketplace distribution The Gemini factory is structured as an end-to-end commercial runway, not just a hackathon: Stage Program pillar Partner benefit 1. Build Seed credits Offset upfront costs: Upfront scoped credits to offset build and porting costs, consumption-based performance credits as partners scale, and scoped engineering support to accelerate development. 2. Launch Cloud marketplace Enable discoverability: Publish directly to Google Cloud Marketplace with streamlined billing, procurement, and enterprise integration to gain direct visibility across global enterprise and mid-market accounts. 3. title: BigQuery measures is now GA: Unifying BI metrics and knowledge graphs for AI accuracy
raw_text:
To answer a complex business question, an AI agent must understand two things: what happened, and why . The what is a governed metric, like revenue at risk; the why is the network of relationships that produced it. Because metric definitions, a.k.a. measures, traditionally live in business intelligence (BI) platforms while relationships live in knowledge graphs, an AI agent only ever sees half the picture. It guesses the rest, leading to confident but sometimes wrong answers. To solve this hallucination problem, we introduced measures in BigQuery , which are now generally available. Historically, organizations needing both BI and knowledge graphs had to run two siloed technology stacks: one to calculate reliable metrics, the other to map out entity relationships. Bridging them entailed brittle data pipelines and runtime reconciliation by analysts and AI agents, who held the connections in their heads or in sprawling prompts. This patchwork approach wasn't just slow and expensive — it’s where data governance broke down, as every analyst and prompt may define joins and metrics differently. Figure 1: A unified model for defining BI metrics and knowledge graphs in one place, for powering AI agents, SQL, GQL and dashboards. To replace manual reconciliation, you need a single model that understands both the structure of your business and the math that measures it. BigQuery measures builds directly on BigQuery Graph to deliver that unified foundation. By defining measures directly on the graph entities they describe, your BI dashboards and AI agents don't just get a number they can trust — they get the relational context behind it. Finally, they can reliably answer both the what and the why . "With BigQuery measures, we can now deliver self-documenting data products. Defining measures natively in BigQuery ensures Looker Dashboards, Conversational Agents and our Data team queries operate on identical logic, guaranteeing metric alignment across leadership and significantly reducing data team maintenance overhead." - Amanda Reelick, Head of Data Enablement, Woolworths NZ One model to answer both the what and the why Let's walk through an example. Suppose your retail bank's risk analytics team spots a sudden spike in transaction activity in the Prague district. You need to know whether this represents healthy customer growth or concentrated risk exposure. Answering requires two pieces of evidence: how much money actually moved (the what ), and which specific accounts it flowed through (the why ). At most banks, getting that answer takes two teams, two tools, and two numbers that are rarely reconciled. With BigQuery, your underlying data is already in place — whether in native tables or in a borderless Lakehouse . With a single schema, you can define a semantic model directly over your existing transaction, account, and district tables — with no data movement and no secondary system: code_block <ListValue: [StructValue([('code', '-- Entities, relationships, and measures, declared in one model
CREATE OR REPLACE PROPERTY GRAPH retail_banking.BankingGraph
 NODE TABLES (
 retail_banking.trans AS Trans
 KEY (trans_id)
 PROPERTIES (
 trans_id, account_id, amount,
 MEASURE(SUM(amount)) AS total_trans_amount
 ),
 retail_banking.account AS Account
 KEY (account_id)
 PROPERTIES (
 account_id, district_id, stmt_frq,
 MEASURE(COUNT(account_id)) AS account_count
 ),
 retail_banking.district AS District
 KEY (district_id)
 PROPERTIES (district_id, city, state)
 )
 EDGE TABLES (
 retail_banking.trans AS POSTED_TO
 KEY (trans_id)
 SOURCE KEY (trans_id) REFERENCES Trans (trans_id)
 DESTINATION KEY (account_id) REFERENCES Account (account_id)
 NO PROPERTIES,
 retail_banking.account AS LOCATED_IN
 KEY (account_id)
 SOURCE KEY (account_id) REFERENCES Account (account_id)
 DESTINATION KEY (district_id) REFERENCES District (district_id)
 NO PROPERTIES
 );'), ('language', ''), ('caption', <wagtail.rich_text.RichText object at 0x7f2f33147a50>)])]> To determine whether the Prague spike reflects broad growth or concentrated exposure, your team checks whether the transaction volume is spread across many accounts or driven by just a few. Using GRAPH_EXPAND , you flatten the graph and roll up both measures with the AGG() function: code_block <ListValue: [StructValue([('code', '-- Volume by city, and the accounts behind it, each counted once
SELECT
 District_city,
 AGG(Trans_total_trans_amount) AS total_volume,
 AGG(Account_account_count) AS accounts_involved
FROM GRAPH_EXPAND("retail_banking.BankingGraph")
GROUP BY District_city;'), ('language', ''), ('caption', <wagtail.rich_text.RichText object at 0x7f2f33145450>)])]> You can ensure accurate reporting by using measures that have been “grain-locked” — where a fixed level of granularity has been assigned to how facts and dimensions are modeled. Because a single account can have thousands of transactions, joining the two tables can duplicate account rows. A standard SQL COUNT(account_id) would overcount those accounts, leaving your risk and finance teams with conflicting numbers. BigQuery measures preserve the native grain of each entity, counting every account only once regardless of how the tables are joined. The second half of the investigation is about connectivity: Which accounts are driving the Prague activity? You can answer that with a traversal in GQL (the ISO-standard Graph Query Language) over the exact same model: code_block <ListValue: [StructValue([('code', "-- Which accounts moved money in Prague
GRAPH retail_banking.BankingGraph
MATCH (:Trans)-[:POSTED_TO]->(a:Account)-[:LOCATED_IN]->(d:District)
WHERE d.city = 'Prague'
RETURN DISTINCT a.account_id"), ('language', ''), ('caption', <wagtail.rich_text.RichText object at 0x7f2f33146a50>)])]> Neither query requires a separate system, and both evaluate against the same governed definitions. New features in BigQuery measures While the preview introduced grain-locked measures tightly integrated with BigQuery Graph, real-world production analytics demand more than basic sums — and enterprise AI agents need programmatic ways to discover and interpret those metrics. The GA of BigQuery measures focuses on two key areas: richer modeling and visualization for complex business logic, and native semantic discovery for the agentic ecosystem. Richer modeling, querying and BI visualization To enable more expressive and flexible measure definitions, MEASURE() supports both composite expressions and derived measures; this capability is GA. Rather than repeating conditional logic across queries, you can define baseline aggregates once and compose them into higher-order calculations on the same table using AGG() . BigQuery validates these formula dependencies at schema compilation time to catch circular references or invalid aggregations early. Downstream dashboards and AI agents can then query complex ratios and net metrics at any dimensionality with consistent accuracy. For example, on your Trans node, you can define settled volume alongside total volume, and then derive unsettled volume and unsettled percentage directly from those building blocks: code_block <ListValue: [StructValue([('code', '-- Compose custom calculations, conditional expressions, and derived ratios
PROPERTIES (
 trans_id, account_id, amount, fee, is_settled,
 MEASURE(SUM(amount)) AS total_trans_amount,
 MEASURE(SUM(CASE WHEN is_settled = TRUE THEN amount ELSE 0.0 END))
 AS settled_volume,
 MEASURE(AVG(CASE WHEN amount > 10000 THEN amount ELSE NULL END))
 AS avg_large_trans,
 -- Derived: written in terms of the measures above
 MEASURE(AGG(total_trans_amount) - AGG(settled_volume)) AS unsettled_volume,
 MEASURE(
 SAFE_DIVIDE(AGG(total_trans_amount) - AGG(settled_volume),
 NULLIF(AGG(total_trans_amount), 0)) * 100.0
 ) AS unsettled_pct
)'), ('language', ''), ('caption', <wagtail.rich_text.RichText object at 0x7f2f33145590>)])]> Query across multiple fact tables Enterprise data models routinely span multiple business processes. Joining separate fact tables that share a common dimension — such as transactions and credit cards linked to the same bank account — traditionally causes a "chasm trap," where cross-fact multiplication inflates both metrics. The new start_node argument in GRAPH_EXPAND solves this by isolating each fact table into its own expansion tree. BigQuery evaluates each measure at its native grain before joining the results on the shared entity: code_block <ListValue: [StructValue([('code', '-- Transactions and cards per account, each evaluated at its own root grain
SELECT
 ET.Account_account_id,
 AGG(ET.Trans_settled_volume) AS settled_volume,
 AGG(EC.Card_card_count) AS total_cards_issued
FROM
 GRAPH_EXPAND("retail_banking.BankingGraph", start_node => "Trans") AS ET
LEFT JOIN
 GRAPH_EXPAND("retail_banking.BankingGraph", start_node => "Card") AS EC
ON ET.Account_account_id = EC.Account_account_id
GROUP BY ET.Account_account_id;'), ('language', ''), ('caption', <wagtail.rich_text.RichText object at 0x7f2f400c8450>)])]> By expanding each fact table from its own root ( Trans and Card ), each branch maintains its exact grain — even for accounts with transactions but no issued cards. Visualize in Data Studio With the updated BigQuery connector in Data Studio , you can now connect directly to BigQuery graphs and build interactive visualizations powered by native measures. Data Studio honors the aggregation logic defined in your graph model, keeping complex calculations consistent across charts while preventing accidental client-side re-aggregations. Built for the agentic era Attach business meaning to your measures In a large enterprise schema, it’s nice to be able to attach business meaning to your measures, as multiple metrics often share similar names. In our banking model alone, total_trans_amount , settled_volume , and unsettled_volume could all casually be called "volume" by a business user. That ambiguity can trip up both analysts building reports and AI agents translating natural-language prompts into SQL. With the GA, you can embed rich semantic metadata directly into each measure definition using the OPTIONS clause, including plain-language description strings, domain synonyms, and custom key-value extensions: code_block <ListValue: [StructValue([('code', "-- Business meaning and governance metadata travel with the metric
MEASURE(SUM(CASE WHEN is_settled = TRUE THEN amount ELSE 0.0 END)) 
 AS settled_volume
 OPTIONS (
 description = 'Transaction value that settled. Excludes fees.',
 synonyms = ['settled amount', 'cleared volume'],
 extensions = [('unit', 'USD'),
 ('owner', 'finance-analytics'),
 ('reporting_tier', 'executive')]
 )"), ('language', ''), ('caption', <wagtail.rich_text.RichText object at 0x7f2f400cbc50>)])]> Because this business context lives inside the schema alongside the SQL formula, your semantic definitions travel wherever the metric is queried. Make measures discoverable to humans and AI agents BigQuery directly integrates with Knowledge Catalog to create a unified discovery and consumption loop for both people and machines: Enterprise-wide context discovery in Knowledge Catalog: BigQuery Graph and measures metadata is automatically ingested and searchable in Knowledge Catalog as a native resource alongside tables, views, and routines. Data stewards, analysts, and AI agents can search across the catalog using business synonyms or descriptions, inspect governance tags, and view the underlying measure’s SQL definitions (such as SUM(CASE WHEN is_settled = TRUE...) ) to verify how each metric is calculated before using it. In Knowledge Catalog, you can also enrich graph metadata with business glossaries and stewardship context, uniting asset discovery, business meaning, and mathematical measures in a single pane so users and agents can work from the same context. Runtime schema introspection in BigQuery: Calling BQ.SHOW_GRAPH_EXPAND_SCHEMA returns an expanded graph's schema as JSON without scanning underlying tables, flagging metrics with "is_measure": true alongside their descriptions and synonyms. Passing flatten_results => FALSE preserves your entity hierarchy as nested ROW ( STRUCT ) types, letting agents inspect the relational tree and query paths like Account.District.city directly. Connect across your data and AI ecosystem Finally, BigQuery measures integrates across the Google Cloud data and AI stack so you can author, reuse, and query semantics in the tools you already use: Author with AI: Use the graph skills in Data Agent Kit to scaffold, author, and validate BigQuery measure definitions using natural-language prompts in your preferred AI coding environment. Reuse existing LookML models: If you already model business metrics in Looker, you can model once using LookML-based derived analytic models to compile Explores, joins, and measures directly into native BigQuery Graph models. Query with natural language: Unified graph and measure definitions are supported out-of-the-box in Conversational Analytics , enabling business users and AI agents to ask complex questions against governed metrics in plain natural language. Get started with BigQuery measures The primary advantage of this unified model is that you can build from the foundation you already have. If you already run a BI semantic layer, take a governed metric and define it directly on the entity it describes; if your foundation is a knowledge graph, attach a unified measure to your most frequent traversal. Whichever side you start from, you are building a single source of truth for both your BI dashboards and your AI agents. To see unified semantics in action, watch the BigQuery measures introduction video , or dive into the BigQuery measures documentation and BigQuery Graph overview . When you are ready to build hands-on, try our step-by-step codelabs for music streaming analytics .

title: Experimenting with ClusterNetworkPolicy in GKE
raw_text:
Standard Network Policies limit you to applying policies at the namespace level, but ClusterNetworkPolicy (CNP) lets you apply granular networking policies across an entire cluster. When you use CNP, you can easily scale security and governance policies. Recently, I experimented with this functionality in Google Kubernetes Engine (GKE) and saw the benefits for myself. In this post, we'll explore using CNP to control traffic to an LLM and cluster. If you want to jump right into a hands-on lab, check out this Codelab: Secure AI Inference Workloads with GKE ClusterNetworkPolicy . How CNP works CNP follows a three-tier flow with a precedence match: Admin tier (top precedence) : Cluster administrator enforces mandatory security rules that can't be bypassed (for example, blocking metadata access). Network policy tier (middle precedence) : Standard namespace-scoped policies that are managed by application teams to control ingress and egress for their microservices. Baseline tier (bottom precedence) : Cluster administrator establishes fallback defaults (for example, a default-deny posture across namespaces). Design pattern example The aim of the experiment in the Codelab is to restrict traffic to the LLM namespace, allow only authorized clients, and prevent cluster-wide access to the metadata API except for DNS port 53. It uses these services: Virtual Private Cloud (VPC) : Provides private networking, subnets for pods and services, and secure outbound egress via Cloud NAT. TPU v5e : High-efficiency accelerator hardware (2x2 topology) running optimized model inference. GKE : Managed Kubernetes platform that's powered by GKE Dataplane V2 (eBPF) to enforce multi-tier networking policies. Gemma 4 ( google/gemma-4-E2B-it ) : Lightweight open model served with vLLM to act as a sensitive AI workload. ClusterNetworkPolicy (CNP) : Cluster-wide policies that let administrators enforce mandatory administrator and baseline guardrails across all namespaces. NetworkPolicies : Standard namespace-scoped rules that let developers grant access to authorized clients. Cloud Logging / GKE Network Policy Logging : Captures real-time packet verdicts ( allow / deny ) and policy audit trails. Putting it together: Setup overview Setting up this environment begins with building a custom private network infrastructure and deploying your TPU-enabled clusters: Custom VPC & Cloud NAT : Establish a custom VPC with a dedicated subnet that hosts primary nodes, plus secondary CIDR IP address ranges for GKE pods ( 10.20.0.0/16 ) and services ( 10.30.0.0/20 ). A Cloud Router and Cloud NAT are configured to handle secure outbound egress for nodes while blocking inbound internet exposure. GKE Standard cluster : Spin up a Standard GKE cluster running GKE Dataplane V2 ( ADVANCED_DATAPATH ). GKE Dataplane V2 acts as the core engine that leverages eBPF under the hood to enforce both standard and cluster-scoped policies dynamically. Dedicated TPU v5e node pool : Provision a node pool featuring ct5lp-hightpu-4t machines arranged in a 2x2 topology slice. The nodes carry a dedicated taint ( google.com/tpu=present:NoSchedule ) to ensure that only accelerator workloads run on them. Deploying the Gemma 4 workload : Isolate the pods by creating three distinct namespaces: gemma-llm ( tier: ai-core ): Serves the lightweight Gemma 4 model using the high-performance vllm/vllm-tpu:latest engine on port 8000. client-ns ( tier: app-frontend ): Runs the authorized chat client that must query the model. untrusted-tenant ( tier: untrusted ): Represents an unauthorized probe container simulating a rogue client. Securing the LLM and metadata: Code walkthrough By default in Kubernetes, all cross-namespace and egress traffic is open. To enforce a defense-in-depth posture, we apply network policies across the GKE evaluation tiers. Step 1: Establish zero-trust posture (baseline tier) To deny all unauthorized ingress cluster-wide, the cluster administrator applies a ClusterNetworkPolicy at the baseline tier. This tier acts as a fallback safety net. code_block <ListValue: [StructValue([('code', 'apiVersion: policy.networking.k8s.io/v1alpha2
kind: ClusterNetworkPolicy
metadata:
 name: baseline-default-deny
spec:
 tier: Baseline
 priority: 1000
 subject:
 namespaces: {}
 ingress:
 - name: allow-dns-ingress
 action: Accept
 from:
 - namespaces: {}
 protocols:
 - udp:
 destinationPort:
 number: 53
 - tcp:
 destinationPort:
 number: 53
 - name: baseline-deny-cross-ns
 action: Deny
 from:
 - namespaces: {}'), ('language', ''), ('caption', <wagtail.rich_text.RichText object at 0x7f2f32979d50>)])]> How it works Precedence placement : Setting tier: Baseline places this policy at the very bottom of the GKE evaluation chain, and the priority: 1000 value orders it within that tier. It only processes traffic that hasn't matched a rule in any higher tier. Global target : Specifying subject.namespaces: {} ensures that this fallback applies globally to every pod in every namespace. DNS isolation exemption : The first ingress rule accepts incoming DNS traffic on TCP and UDP port 53. Without this explicit exemption, cluster-wide DNS resolution would fail. Fallback deny : The second rule matches any incoming pod-to-pod connection attempt and drops it. At this stage, both the client-ns and untrusted-tenant namespaces are blocked from contacting Gemma. Step 2: Delegate access to developers (networkpolicy tier) With the baseline default-deny active, the application team that manages gemma-llm can safely delegate access to legitimate clients. They define a standard namespace-scoped NetworkPolicy to allow incoming port 8000 traffic from rag-agent pods in the client-ns namespace. code_block <ListValue: [StructValue([('code', 'apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: NetworkPolicy
metadata:
 name: allow-rag-client
 namespace: gemma-llm
spec:
 podSelector:
 matchLabels:
 app: gemma-service
 policyTypes:
 - Ingress
 ingress:
 # Explicitly permit ingress only from pods matching app: rag-agent in client-ns
 - from:
 - namespaceSelector:
 matchLabels:
 kubernetes.io/metadata.name: client-ns
 podSelector:
 matchLabels:
 app: rag-agent
 ports:
 - protocol: TCP
 port: 8000'), ('language', ''), ('caption', <wagtail.rich_text.RichText object at 0x7f2f32668e50>)])]> How it works Developer control : This resource resides within the gemma-llm namespace and it's managed directly by the developer, matching the GKE focus on operational separation. Middle precedence matching : Standard Kubernetes NetworkPolicies map directly to the NetworkPolicy Tier. Because this tier is evaluated before the baseline tier, incoming TCP packets from the authorized client to port 8000 match this rule and are immediately accepted. Fall-through block : Connections that originate from the untrusted-tenant namespace fail to match this rule, pass through to the baseline tier, and are dropped. Step 3: Enforce global egress guardrails (admin tier) By default, Pods can query the GKE link-local Compute Engine metadata server ( 169.254.169.254 ). Those queries expose instance metadata and potentially high-privilege service account tokens. To lock this down, the cluster administrator applies an egress guardrail at the highest tier in the GKE hierarchy. code_block <ListValue: [StructValue([('code', 'apiVersion: policy.networking.k8s.io/v1alpha2
kind: ClusterNetworkPolicy
metadata:
 name: admin-global-guardrails
spec:
 tier: Admin
 priority: 10
 subject:
 namespaces: {} # Targets every namespace in the cluster
 ingress:
 # Delegate all ingress decisions down to developer and baseline tiers
 - name: delegate-all-ingress
 action: Pass
 from:
 - namespaces: {}
 egress:
 # Allow DNS resolution so pods can locate endpoints
 - name: allow-all-dns
 action: Accept
 to:
 - networks:
 - 0.0.0.0/0
 protocols:
 - udp:
 destinationPort:
 number: 53
 - tcp:
 destinationPort:
 number: 53
 # Hard deny on the Compute Engine metadata server
 - name: block-metadata-server-global
 action: Deny
 to:
 - networks:
 - 169.254.169.254/32
 # Delegate remaining egress traffic to lower tiers
 - name: delegate-other-egress
 action: Pass
 to:
 - namespaces: {}'), ('language', ''), ('caption', <wagtail.rich_text.RichText object at 0x7f2f329345d0>)])]> How it works Admin tier precedence : Deploying this policy in the admin tier ensures that it's evaluated first, and priority 10 orders it within that tier. GKE processes this policy before standard NetworkPolicies and baseline rules. Controlled delegation : The delegate-all-ingress and delegate-other-egress rules have an action: Pass directive that instructs the engine to forward evaluation down to the next tier for remaining in-cluster traffic. Inviolable guardrail : When any pod attempts to query 169.254.169.254/32 on non-DNS ports, the query matches the block-metadata-server-global rule and it's dropped. Because this drop occurs at the top admin tier, it can't be bypassed or overridden, even if a namespace developer deploys an allow-all egress policy. Verifying with Observability for GKE Verifying and auditing security policies is straightforward using the built-in telemetry capabilities of GKE Dataplane V2: Hubble eBPF streams : Provides real-time, kernel-level packet inspection without injecting sidecars. Administrators can stream live network flows to observe policy verdicts as they happen, making it easy to validate allowed communication paths and identify dropped packets immediately. GKE Network Logging and Cloud Logging : Automatically exports structured connection telemetry and policy enforcement verdicts directly into Cloud Logging. Teams can filter and alert on policy decisions using attributes such as disposition="deny" , source/destination namespaces, and jsonPayload.policies[0].name to maintain audit compliance and investigate blocked connection attempts. CNP can be useful and, as always, when you use it in your production environment, you'll need to plan and design the rules based on your setup. Next steps Take a deeper dive and find more information on these features: ClusterNetworkPolicy in GKE: Balancing control and autonomy for your microservices Configuring GKE ClusterNetworkPolicy Want to ask a question, find out more, or share a thought? Connect with me on LinkedIn !
summary: Standard Network Policies limit you to applying policies at the namespace level, but ClusterNetworkPolicy (CNP) lets you apply granular networking policies across an entire cluster. When you use CNP, you can easily scale security and governance policies. Recently, I experimented with this functionality in Google Kubernetes Engine (GKE) and saw the benefits for myself. In this post, we'll explore using CNP to control traffic to an LLM and cluster.

title: Choosing QuePaxa, an unusual consensus algorithm
raw_text: Cloudflare is building an experimental consensus service using a never-before-deployed consensus algorithm, QuePaxa. In this post we explain how QuePaxa works and why we chose it.
