title: Commvault rolls out an automated recovery mechanism, promising faster restoration of business
raw_text: Commvault on Tuesday rolled out its answer to enterprise backup restoration nightmares. Called Recovery Studio, the vendor promised that the product would “orchestrate the recovery of applications, identities, configurations, infrastructure dependencies, and datasets together in an automated, runbook-driven workflow.” Analysts and consultants applauded the effort, agreeing that enterprises today struggle with fast, accurate and secure restorations. But they also stressed that the new system, which is targeted for early access in December with general availability “in the coming months,” places the onus on IT to keep a dependency map current. Recovery Studio isn’t using any form of AI to figure out proper restoration details. It relies on a map of assets, dependencies, and other relevant information that the customer creates and maintains, and for many enterprises, the challenge of keeping such a document current is the real problem. Even discounting the times when a line of business doesn’t tell IT about an application change, IT teams struggle to keep up with the speed of change in the organization. Commvault’s news release said that its automation allows businesses to “say goodbye to manual and painstaking attempts to restore complicated business services in a fragmented fashion that can result in downtime and data loss.” It pointed out that a large enterprise may need to restore hundreds of applications and thousands of identities, including the configurations and underlying data, all in the right order at the right time. “It’s no wonder that with conventional approaches, recovery to even a minimal level of operation takes an average of 28 days,” the release said. Commvault said Recovery Studio can manage a wide range of components that go beyond containers, VMs, files, and objects, extending to identity systems, application configurations, infrastructure configurations and security and network settings. It also promised that the Recovery Studio can standardize “across all recovery scenarios” including “operational, disaster and cyber recoveries. Unified runbooks automate infrastructure rebuilds, workload recovery, and the orchestration of security controls, such as firewall rules and network security groups and settings – all actions needed to rebuild the business, not just recover data.” The news release said that the new application can deliver other cybersecurity assistance via data security checks, including “automated threat scanning for supported resources in the runbook to identify compromised areas and inform recovery decisions before returning services to production.” Commvault did not provide a spokesperson to offer further details before publication. Depends on IT awareness of the environment A number of factors will influence the effectiveness of the solution, analysts said. Frank Dickson , principal analyst at Dickson Research, pointed out, “nothing in Commvault’s announcement describes a generative model making recovery decisions. This is runbook automation. A runbook is a recipe: do this, then this, then this. It does not hallucinate. It does exactly what it is told.” “That is the real risk. A flawed runbook gets executed flawlessly, at machine speed,” he said. “Automation does not make a bad plan good. It makes a bad plan fast.” That means, said Aman Mahapatra , chief strategy officer for New York City-based technology consulting firm Tribeca Softech, whether Recovery Studio ultimately helps or hurts enterprise restoration efforts depends on how aware IT is of everything going on in its global footprint. “How much it solves depends on something no vendor controls, which is the accuracy of the dependency map underneath it. A runbook is a prediction about your environment and every change since it was last tested makes it a little more wrong: a new application, a rotated certificate, a firewall rule added on a Friday,” Mahapatra said. “Most enterprise dependency maps are aspirational,” he noted, “and CMDBs in particular tend to describe the environment someone intended to build. Commvault’s figure of 28 days to reach minimal operations is plausible, but the gains will go to organizations that refresh and rehearse their runbooks continuously. For everyone else, automation will execute an outdated plan faster.” Abbas Jaffery , principal advisory director at Infotech, agreed. “My concern is that automation can execute the wrong recovery sequence just as efficiently as the right one. Enterprise environments change constantly,” Jaffery said. “Applications are upgraded, infrastructure moves, identities change and integrations are added or removed. If the dependency information behind a recovery workflow is outdated, automation could restore systems successfully but leave the business service broken.” Defined recovery Mike Leone , a VP and principal analyst at Moor Insights & Strategy, added that Commvault is still advancing the space. Recovery Studio “follows defined recovery runbooks rather than a model inventing steps on the fly. That’s much more deterministic and structured,” Leone said. “Sure, automation can repeat a mistake faster than a person can, and a runbook that’s gone stale is a fair concern. But Commvault is validating each piece as it rebuilds and scanning for threats before anything goes back into production. Those are the kind of safeguards and checks everyone should want. The alternative is people rebuilding systems by hand in the middle of an outage, and that isn’t exactly mistake-free either.” But Dickson stressed that automation is not necessarily the perfect fix. “Commvault says the runbooks validate components and can scan supported resources for threats before services return to production. Good,” he said. “But the honest comparison is not automation versus perfection. It is automation versus exhausted people working from a spreadsheet at 3 a.m. Humans get the order wrong, too.” Johnny Yu , an IDC research manager, is not as impressed by the components of the solution as he is by the way Recovery Studio organizes them. “I do see Commvault Recovery Studio as significant, but not from a capability standpoint,” Yu said, adding that all of the product’s components, including recovery runbooks, threat scans, and recovery testing, are already offered by Commvault, as well as by various competitors. “I think the significance comes from how Recovery Studio organizes different recovery workflows for different applications onto a single platform or hub, kind of like a library of validated recovery runbooks to be used for all kinds of scenarios.” He explained that he liked how Studio standardizes recovery runbooks to follow a similar workflow to that of manually rebuilding the environment, recovering the components, such as data, applications and agents, and “validating the recovery before bringing it back into production, but allows recovery nuance for each runbook, such as if you want to do in-place vs secondary-site recovery or whether threat scanning is necessary, such as DR scenario vs cyber recovery scenario.” Jaffery noted, however, that while the promised Commvault cybersecurity controls are attractive, they may also be insufficient. “Following a cyberattack, organizations need to be confident they aren’t restoring compromised identities, configurations or malicious persistence mechanisms,” Jaffery said. “I would not advocate fully autonomous recovery for every scenario. There needs to be appropriate human authorization for high-impact actions, particularly those involving identity, security controls and reconnecting systems to production. And organizations need to test the entire recovery process, not just whether the backup can be restored.” An AI agent recovery plan Commvault on Tuesday also introduced AgentRecover capabilities to help track and control autonomous agents. It would specifically “help organizations audit agent activity, restore agents, and recover the data and systems they affected across environments.” Mahapatra noted that AgentRecover addresses a potentially more difficult problem than system restorations. “Restoring an agent’s configuration is straightforward. Unwinding what it did is not, because an agent’s actions land as side effects in other systems, and some of them, such as an email sent or a payment initiated, cannot be restored at all,” Mahapatra said. “Traditional recovery rolls back to a point in time,” he explained. “Rolling an environment back to 9 a.m. erases everyone’s legitimate work since 9 a.m., while rolling back only what the agent changed requires knowing causality: which agent, acting under which identity, changed which record. Commvault’s mapping of agent activity and the identities agents act through points in the right direction.” Jaffery added that rollbacks of an autonomous agent can be especially daunting. “Restoring the agent itself doesn’t necessarily undo what it has done. An agent might modify customer records, change permissions, invoke APIs or trigger downstream transactions,” he said. “You need to understand what actions it performed and what the consequences were before deciding what to reverse or restore.” Leone also noted that agents can complicate system restoration, partially because of their speed. “Agents don’t wait for anyone to confirm things are safe. The moment a system comes back, agents start hitting it, far faster than any person would,” he said. “If an agent comes back before the data and identities it relies on are verified, it starts acting on stale or incomplete information at machine speed. Get the order wrong and one outage quickly turns into a second one.” Jaffery also observed that Commvault is far from alone in the automated restoration space, and may even be a tad late. “I don’t think Commvault has an uncontested position here. Rubrik, Cohesity and Veeam have all been investing in cyber recovery, application recovery and orchestration,” he said. “Rubrik, in particular, has been pushing toward automated business application recovery and dependency mapping. Cohesity has capabilities around cyber recovery orchestration and cloud application reconstruction, while Veeam has an established disaster recovery orchestration offering.” This article originally appeared on NetworkWorld .
summary: Commvault on Tuesday rolled out its answer to enterprise backup restoration nightmares. Called Recovery Studio, the vendor promised that the product would “orchestrate the recovery of applications, identities, configurations, infrastructure dependencies, and datasets together in an automated, runbook-driven workflow.” Analysts and consultants applauded the effort, agreeing that enterprises today struggle with fast, accurate and secure restorations. But they also stressed that the new system, which is targeted for early access in December with general availability “in the coming months,” places the onus on IT to keep a dependency map current. Recovery Studio isn’t using any form of AI to figure out proper restoration details.

title: Finite State Raises $27 Million to Help Device Makers Fight ‘Vulnpocalypse’ with AI-Powered Product Security
raw_text: Funding Will Scale Finite State’s Autonomous Platform and International Expansion as Manufacturers Face a Surge of AI-Discovered Flaws and New Global Security Mandates Finite State , a leader in product security and software supply chain risk management, today announced a $27 million Series C funding round led by private funds managed by The O.H.I.O. Fund, with participation from CIBC Innovation Banking, Energy Impact Partners, Energize Capital, and National Grid Partners to continue its mission to secure the world’s connected devices. Finite State’s AI-driven product security platform analyzes the software and firmware inside finished devices, giving manufacturers visibility into the products they build and sell, from vehicles and medical devices to industrial equipment, consumer electronics and critical utility infrastructure. The platform uncovers both known and zero-day vulnerabilities and guides manufacturers in fixing the exploitable ones before attackers strike, making everyday life safer and more secure. The new capital will expand Finite State’s already global operations, deepen its presence across key international markets, and accelerate development of the platform’s autonomous capabilities. These investments will enable more manufacturers around the world to uncover the gap between the software they plan to ship and what actually runs in the finished device, and to continuously identify and mitigate security risks across increasingly complex software supply chains. The funding comes at a turning point for product security. In October, AI-powered research uncovered critical flaws in some of the world’s most widely used software, including a vulnerability in the PHP programming language that underpins much of the web, in a surge security leaders have dubbed the “Vulnpocalypse.” AI has shrunk the time it takes to find a flaw and turn it into an attack from weeks to days, and sometimes hours. Connected devices are especially exposed: a single flaw in a shared open-source component can sit inside millions of shipped products that are hard to inventory and slow to patch. For manufacturers, the urgent question is no longer whether a vulnerability exists. It is which of their products contain it. In parallel, regulators worldwide now expect connected products to be secure by design, with security built in and demonstrated before a device ships rather than added after it reaches the market. The EU Cyber Resilience Act, FDA premarket cybersecurity requirements, UNECE R155 and R156 for vehicles, and IEC 62443 for industrial systems all place the burden of proof on the manufacturer, and the cost of falling short includes blocked market access, recalls, and liability. Meeting that standard is difficult because modern connected products are assembled, not written from scratch. A single device can contain open source libraries, third-party components, and legacy code from many suppliers, and what ships in the finished firmware often differs from what the source code and bill of materials describe. Manufacturers cannot secure what they cannot see. “Every connected product—cars, infusion pumps, toys, OT, baby monitors, your home router—runs on third-party code and components, making inspection and security exceptionally challenging,” said Mike Venerable, Founding Partner, The O.H.I.O. Fund . “Governments worldwide are imposing new regulatory pressures on manufacturers, recognizing how quickly AI-enabled attackers can exploit vulnerabilities. Finite State is solving an incredibly difficult product and technology security challenge by deploying a platform that has earned the trust of investors and customers. We are delighted to support Finite State through this financing and believe the company will be an important solution for connected device security and supply chain risk mitigation.”“Moments like this separate the companies built for what’s coming from those still catching up,” said Brittany Blanco, Innovation Banking Director II, CIBC Innovation Banking . “We’re excited to back a team that saw this shift early and is ready to meet it on a global scale.” Finite State customers span the world’s critical infrastructure and connected device ecosystem—from national power grids and a U.S. national security research laboratory to global automakers, life-saving medical devices, and the connected hardware running inside homes, hospitals, and factories worldwide. With the IoT security market projected to reach $80.3 billion by 2031, [1] Finite State’s growing international customer base reflects a challenge that increasingly transcends borders: manufacturers must understand exactly what software is inside their products, whether it can be exploited, and what they need to do about it. Bruce Lin, Senior Manager, Software Department at JET OPTOELECTRONICS CO., LTD. , a Tier 1 supplier of automotive electronics and smart cockpit solutions serving global automakers, said: “The depth of Finite State’s binary and firmware analysis, the insight it yields into what’s in a shipped device and not just the build manifest, the direct and transitive dependency visibility, and audit-ready compliance mapped to the regulations we actually face, are all invaluable.” Finite State founder and CEO Matt Wyckhouse said: “The Vulnpocalypse isn’t a one-month event. It’s the new baseline. AI-equipped attackers can now find a flaw faster than most manufacturers can figure out which of their products contain it. Governments are rightly advancing regulations to protect the public good, leaving security teams to prove that risks they identify are understood and addressed. Finite State delivers the evidence, intelligence, and automation to protect manufacturers, organizations, and consumers. This Series C round will enable our talented team to both drive the next generation of remarkable platform advances and expand our global reach to safeguard both our customers and theirs.” Among its latest honors, Finite State was named to the 2026 Inc. 5000, an annual ranking of the fastest-growing private companies in America, and chosen as a finalist in SiliconANGLE’s prestigious 2026 TechForward Awards in the Security category. Leveraging deep binary analysis and AI-native execution, the platform unifies code, compiled components, and firmware in minutes—connecting security design with deployed software. By continuously generating SBOMs, VEX, and signed compliance packages, Finite State enables connected device companies across industries such as medical devices and automotive to meet evolving regulations, including the EU Cyber Resilience Act (CRA), and deliver continuous compliance at speed. title: November 2026 Patch Tuesday: 63 Critical Microsoft fixes, plus an Outlook zero day that allows theft of hashed credentials
raw_text: A currently exploited zero-day vulnerability that can let attackers steal hashed Outlook NTLM credentials is among the 1,094 holes Microsoft fixed in its November Patch Tuesday releases. Although rated as only moderate in severity, with a CVSS score of 6.5, Windows administrators need to address CVE-2026-124194 immediately because threat actors are already attacking it. “Don’t let the low score fool you,” said Nick Carroll, cyber incident response manager at Nightwing. Affected products include Microsoft 365 Apps for Enterprise, and Office LTSC 2021 and 2024. However, since the user has to open a malicious Office file to launch the attack, good employee cybersecurity awareness training and an effective email gateway could mitigate this attack until the patch is installed. Opening the malicious file could cause Outlook to connect to an attacker-controlled network location without displaying the usual external-content warning, potentially disclosing authentication information that could be used to impersonate the user. The vulnerability discloses a user’s NTLMv2 password hash to the attacker, who may be able to relay it to other systems to sign in as the user, or crack it to recover the password. Microsoft, which has been using its AI model to find thousands of vulnerabilities in its products since the summer, credited an Anthropic researcher using the Claude AI assistant for finding the Outlook vulnerability. That led Satyam Narang , senior staff researcher at Tenable, to comment, “for most of the year, AI has been building bigger haystacks across Patch Tuesday releases, and this appears to be the first time it has found a needle.” Separately, SAP plugged a critical memory corruption vulnerability dubbed ICM2Shell, with a CVSS rating of 10. Discovered by researchers at Onapsis, the vulnerability impacts the way the SAP Kernel handles WebSocket traffic. Onapsis said that a specially crafted sequence of WebSocket messages could either crash a process or allow an attacker to run code remotely. Affected are SAP Internet Communications Manager (ICM), which is inside the kernel, and SAP Web Dispatcher, a reverse proxy many organizations place at the edge of their network. Microsoft patches Of the 1,094 Microsoft vulnerabilities, 63 were rated as critical. Four flaws carry a CVSS severity score of 9.8, noted Jack Bicer , director of vulnerability research at Action1, and three of them need no credentials and no user action to exploit. The Windows LDAP Remote Code Execution Vulnerability ( CVE-2026-119958 ) lets an unauthenticated attacker run code inside the Windows LDAP service, which puts domain controllers and the whole Active Directory environment at risk. The Microsoft Exchange Server Remote Code Execution Vulnerability ( CVE-2026-118207 ) can be triggered by anyone able to send email to the organization, Bicer said, and the Windows Xbox Live Networking Service Remote Code Execution Vulnerability ( CVE-2026-112967 ) gives an attacker on the same network full control of a Windows system. The fourth, the Azure OpenAI Elevation of Privilege Vulnerability ( CVE-2026-119990 ), sits in a cloud service many teams now depend on. However, this service is automatically patched by Microsoft. Patch order should follow reach, not product names, Bicer advised CSOs. Domain controllers and Exchange servers go first, he said, followed by anything that exposes IIS, Microsoft Secure Channel (Schannel) or RPC to untrusted networks. Message Queuing deserves an inventory before it gets a patch: find every server where the service is enabled, turn it off where no application needs it, and patch the rest the same day, he said, adding that hypervisor hosts need their own maintenance window, because one escaped guest becomes a problem for every tenant on that host. “What defenders need to know and do right now is abandon broad triage and take immediate defensive action,” said Dustin Childs , head of threat awareness at TrendAI’s Zero Day Initiative. That means first patching Exchange and domain controllers (meaning LDAP/Kerberos) to stop zero-click compromise, ring-fence exposed network services like DNS and DHCP to prevent wormable spread, and verify manual administrative fixes on cloud services your organization uses. Tyler Reguly , associate director of security R&D at Fortra, observed that there are fewer Microsoft vulnerabilities this month than there were in October, but noted, “I’m not foolish enough to think that this single drop indicates that we’re into the downward trend that I predicted we’ll see in the coming months. Instead, I think that we’re seeing a continuation of the elevated numbers as Microsoft continues to fix long hidden issues that are being surfaced by AI. Soon, however, these numbers will begin to decline as the last of these long-hidden issues are resolved and we only have new bugs to deal with.” CSOs can help their teams by ignoring any noise coming from vendors and any vulnerabilities that are overhyped, Reguly said. When vulnerability counts started to rise, it was C-level employees who jumped up the fastest and added to the burden their admins were facing. “Now it’s time to settle down and support your teams rather than increasing their burden. CSOs should keep in mind that AI companies and security vendors may needlessly hype unimportant vulnerabilities because it is cheap, effective marketing for their services,” he pointed out. “A vulnerability isn’t critical if you don’t have the impacted software deployed.” Prevention is key, so CSOs should focus their efforts on system hardening and mitigation. This, he said, will be more effective than chasing vulnerabilities. Finally, Reguly reminded CSOs that prioritization matters. “If you’ve developed a prioritization strategy that works for you, don’t change your process just because the media is looking for clicks,” he said. SAP patches The critical vulnerabilities collectively known as ICM2Shell are CVE-2026-76964 and CVE-2026-89126 . Researchers at Onapsis, who discovered them, said exploitation isn’t theoretical; they provided SAP with a working exploit that achieves full, unauthenticated remote code execution end to end, running arbitrary commands as adm on the target system. The denial-of-service condition, in turn, reproduced on every SAP Kernel release tested. To access the flaw, an attacker only needs network access to the HTTP/HTTPS port, says Onapsis. Because WebSocket support is enabled by default in both the ICM and the SAP Web Dispatcher, a system is exposed even if no application uses WebSocket. Some services, including default ICF services in SAP S/4HANA, accept WebSocket connections without authentication, and in others the flaw can be reached before authentication takes place. “Nothing in the chain requires an SAP user, a password or a certificate,” the researchers said. The adm account owns the SAP installation, the researchers pointed out, including its executables, its instance profiles, its secure store, and its connection to the database. Running commands as that user grants full control of the SAP system. An attacker could, among other things recover database credentials and other secrets from the secure store and profiles and use them to read or alter any business data directly in the database; collect RFC destinations and technical credentials that let them move on to the SAP and non-SAP systems connected to this one; change configuration or binaries to keep persistent access; and destroy data. Other patches Chris Goettl , VP of product management at Ivanti, drew attention to patches from Adobe, Mozilla and Google. Adobe released nine security bulletins that resolve 110 CVEs, 22 of which are critical. Adobe said it is not aware of any exploits in the wild. The two Priority 2 updates carry the most risk; Connect (APSB26-191) has the largest count at 24 CVEs, 18 of them critical and six rated CVSS 10.0. The vulnerabilities span SSRF, path traversal and SQL injection, and affect Windows on-prem versions 12.12 and earlier. The Experience Manager (APSB26-189) patch fixes 14 CVEs, including four Critical code execution flaws rated CVSS 9.9. Google Chrome 157.0.8103.50, released on Monday, resolved nine CVEs including CVE-2026-125350 , which is being actively exploited in the wild. This marks Chrome’s eighth zero-day exploit of 2026, Goettl noted. Chromium-based browsers such as Microsoft Edge will need the fix as well, and users should relaunch after updating for the patch to take effect. This patched release follows Chrome 157’s November 3 release, which fixed 213 vulnerabilities, seven of them critical. Separately, Google’s November Android bulletin fixed 216 vulnerabilities, 23 of them critical, with none marked as exploited. The target is patch level is 2026-11-05 or later. Mozilla’s November 10 release includes Firefox 160, which resolves 99 CVEs (57 of them are ranked High). Firefox ESR 153.7 resolves 81 vulnerabilities. (51 High), and ESR 115.45 resolves 28, all High. Many of the High-rated issues are use-after-free and memory boundary flaws across graphics, DOM, layout, and JavaScript components, including a number of sandbox escapes such as CVE-2026-124907 , a use-after-free in CanvasWebGL that allows privilege escalation and sandbox escape. The same flaw is addressed in Thunderbird 160 and Thunderbird 153.7.
summary: A currently exploited zero-day vulnerability that can let attackers steal hashed Outlook NTLM credentials is among the 1,094 holes Microsoft fixed in its November Patch Tuesday releases. Although rated as only moderate in severity, with a CVSS score of 6.5, Windows administrators need to address CVE-2026-124194 immediately because threat actors are already attacking it. “Don’t let the low score fool you,” said Nick Carroll, cyber incident response manager at Nightwing. Affected products include Microsoft 365 Apps for Enterprise, and Office LTSC 2021 and 2024.

title: N-able N-central gets emergency fix two days after 33 exploits published
raw_text: N-able has taken its hosted N-central remote monitoring and management (RMM) platform offline worldwide and shipped an emergency hotfix after a security researcher released 33 zero-day exploits for the software, including attack chains that could let unauthenticated attackers take over servers. N-central is used by managed service providers (MSPs) and enterprise IT teams to remotely manage, patch, and support endpoint systems, so a compromised server can expose every computer under its control. N-able said it took the hosted environments offline as a precaution and advised customers using the on-premises version to shut down their servers until it released the fix, N-central 2026.4 HF2 , on Tuesday. The vulnerabilities were disclosed late Sunday by an offensive security researcher named Sean Bales who uses the GitHub handle Oracle-Security. The release includes proof-of-concept exploit chains that require no authentication and could result in command execution as the service account and, in some cases, root access. N-able said it has already observed scanning activity associated with the published exploits but has not seen evidence that any customer environment has been successfully exploited. Censys found 1,728 internet-exposed N-central instances , and security firm Previdian recorded 68 exploitation attempts against one of its honeypots from a single IP address within about 18 hours of the publication. Exploit chains lead to remote code execution The 33 exploits , which the researcher dubbed Able2Shell, are organized into four attack chains. The most severe requires no authentication and abuses an XML external entity (XXE) flaw in a service-import function to steal a trusted local session, reset an account password, and execute commands as the nable service user. The same chain can create a Default Administrator account with credentials chosen by the attacker, giving them full control of the appliance. Two other attack chains start from a predictable appliance passcode that lets an anonymous attacker inject malicious patch metadata. When an administrator opens the patch details, a stored cross-site scripting (XSS) payload runs in their browser and invokes a command-execution interface as the nable user. The administrator’s session can also be hijacked through the same flaw to submit a crafted audit-export configuration that runs commands as root. A fourth chain writes an executable web page into the server’s web directory through a directory traversal flaw in a software repository feature, then escalates to root through a passwordless installer that executes a configuration from a directory the nable user can write to. Bales tested all of the exploits against N-central Appliance 2026.4.0.31, a pre-release build, and noted in the repository’s documentation that most, if not all, of the flaws should work on previous versions, including the most up-to-date release. N-able has not confirmed how many of the 33 flaws it could reproduce, but the new hotfix lists 7 CVEs: CVE-2026-125883 — Multiple XXE vulnerabilities CVE-2026-125878 — Multiple OGNL injection vulnerabilities CVE-2026-125879 — Local privilege escalation to root via nable-writable syslog-ng config CVE-2026-125880 — Stored XSS via MMS3 patch metadata (admin context) CVE-2026-125881 — Schema-hint SSRF via service import schema validation CVE-2026-125882 — RCE via file repository upload path traversal (Credit Nate Fair, Sprocket Security) CVE-2026-91000 — Insecure IPC Channels lead to local privilege escalation Attacks likely to follow N-central has been targeted by attackers in the past and the Able2Shell disclosure is the fourth time in 15 months that N-able has been forced to do an emergency response. In August 2025, the company patched two flaws tracked as CVE-2025-8875 and CVE-2025-8876 that were exploited in the wild as zero-days. In August this year, the company patched an authentication bypass flaw tracked as CVE-2026-18556 that was exploited as a zero-day to deploy ransomware, but the patch was incomplete and attackers quickly found a bypass: CVE-2026-18577. Microsoft attributed the ransomware attacks that abused the flaw to Storm-1175, a financially motivated group linked to China that deployed the StormEncryptor ransomware on MSP-managed systems. In September, security firm Huntress discovered that a fully patched N-central server had been compromised through a new chain of access-control flaws tracked as CVE-2026-86206 and CVE-2026-86207. A day later N-able disclosed CVE-2026-86218, a pre-authentication remote code execution flaw rated 10.0 on the CVSS scale that had also been exploited. N-able claims more than 25,000 MSP partners and telemetry from more than 11 million endpoints. What customers should do With the N-central 2026.4 Hotfix 2 available, N-able said on-premises customers should upgrade as soon as possible, and all customers — hosted and on-premises — must upgrade their Agents and Probes to restore compatibility between the two. Security firm Huntress advised N-central administrators to review authentication activity from Nov. 8 onward, look for administrator accounts, scripts, and remote-access sessions they did not create, and assess every client network managed by the server, not just the server itself. Huntress also cautioned that patched servers may not display a new version number, so administrators should verify fixes against N-able’s guidance rather than the version string. ThreatDefence recommended preserving logs and server snapshots before making any changes, then rotating credentials for administrator and technician accounts, asset-discovery databases, agent registration tokens, and ecosystem agent keys once the server is restored.
summary: N-able has taken its hosted N-central remote monitoring and management (RMM) platform offline worldwide and shipped an emergency hotfix after a security researcher released 33 zero-day exploits for the software, including attack chains that could let unauthenticated attackers take over servers. N-central is used by managed service providers (MSPs) and enterprise IT teams to remotely manage, patch, and support endpoint systems, so a compromised server can expose every computer under its control. N-able said it took the hosted environments offline as a precaution and advised customers using the on-premises version to shut down their servers until it released the fix, N-central 2026.4 HF2 , on Tuesday. The vulnerabilities were disclosed late Sunday by an offensive security researcher named Sean Bales who uses the GitHub handle Oracle-Security.

title: Syntys breaks ground on 20MW Qatar datacentre as AI infrastructure investment gathers pace
raw_text:
Syntys has begun construction on a 20MW (megawatt) datacentre in Qatar, part of the broader expansion of digital infrastructure in the country as demand for cloud computing, artificial intelligence (AI) and high-performance computing (HPC) rises across the Middle East.

The investment comes as Qatar seeks to strengthen its position as a regional technology hub, with digital infrastructure becoming an increasingly important part of its economic diversification and national development strategy.

The development also follows MWC26 Doha, which brought together more than 10,000 participants from 100 countries on 8 to 10 November. The event provided a platform for government leaders, telecommunications operators and technology companies to discuss the future of AI, next-generation connectivity and digital economies. 

For Qatar, the discussions at MWC Doha highlighted the importance of moving beyond technology adoption towards building the infrastructure, capabilities and partnerships required to support a more advanced digital economy.

Expanding Qatar’s datacentre ecosystem

The new Syntys facility forms part of the company’s strategy to expand its Qatar operations through a combination of acquisitions and new developments.

Earlier this year, Syntys acquired QData QFZ LLC, adding two operational, Tier III-compliant, carrier-neutral datacentre facilities to its portfolio. With the latest development, the company now owns and operates four campuses in Qatar, allowing customers to establish primary and disaster recovery environments across separate locations within the country.

The new facility is being developed on an existing Syntys campus, where power infrastructure, fibre connectivity and an established operations team are already in place. This is intended to accelerate the delivery of additional capacity while building on existing operational capabilities.

Designed to be Tier III-compliant, the facility will accommodate different rack densities, including higher-density configurations required for GPU-accelerated AI and HPC workloads.

As organisations move AI applications from experimentation into production, the underlying infrastructure requirements are changing. Generative AI, large language models and other compute-intensive applications require greater processing capacity, higher power densities and specialised cooling capabilities.

Cloud platforms are also becoming a primary route through which businesses access AI, whether through embedded features in enterprise software or tools used by developers to build new applications.

According to Mordor Intelligence, the Middle East hyperscale datacentre market is forecast to grow at a compound annual growth rate of 23.5% between 2025 and 2031, reflecting the increasing investment in infrastructure needed to support the region’s digital ambitions.

“Qatar is our home market, and we are seeing demand here translate into larger, denser and more varied deployments,” said Sunita Bottse, chief executive officer of Syntys.

“We are investing to meet that demand and designing this capacity for the densities our customers are moving toward.”

The facility will operate under a carrier-neutral model, allowing customers to select their connectivity providers and design network resilience according to their individual requirements.

Syntys already designs and operates the facilities hosting Ooredoo’s sovereign AI cloud, powered by Nvidia Hopper GPUs. The new development builds on the company’s experience in supporting high-density computing environments.

For Ooredoo, the investment is part of a wider effort to strengthen the digital infrastructure underpinning Qatar’s technology ambitions.

“Digital infrastructure is the nation-building foundation of the modern economy,” said Aziz Aluthman Fakhroo, group chief executive officer of Ooredoo Group.

“I am proud of Syntys’s latest milestone investment, which reinforces Qatar’s capacity for cloud computing, AI and advanced digital services. Ultimately, the success of digital transformation will be measured by the opportunities we create for businesses, talent and future generations.”

Qatar’s Digital Agenda 2030 puts infrastructure at the centre

The development comes as Qatar advances its Digital Agenda 2030, the national strategy designed to accelerate the country’s transition towards a digitally driven economy.

The agenda identifies digital infrastructure as one of six strategic pillars, alongside digital government, digital technologies, innovation, the digital economy and digital society.

Qatar aims to generate approximately QAR40bn in cumulative economic impact from its digital transformation ambitions by 2030, while creating 26,000 jobs in the ICT sector.

Building the infrastructure to support these objectives is becoming increasingly important as government entities and businesses deploy AI applications, migrate workloads to cloud environments and digitise services across sectors including healthcare, financial services, energy, education and transport.

The country’s approach was particularly visible at MWC26 Doha, where the Qatar Pavilion brought together more than 15 government and semi-government organisations to demonstrate national digital initiatives.

Projects showcased included the Government Artificial Intelligence Programme, digital government services, the TASMU Smart Qatar Programme and AI-powered applications across justice, labour, commerce and environmental services.

The demonstrations reflected a broader shift towards integrating AI and data into public services, improving operational efficiency and developing digital solutions that can be deployed across the economy.

The government also highlighted the next phase of Qatar’s Tasmu smart city programme, which includes six upcoming national solutions powered by data and AI, alongside innovation and accelerator programmes supporting the development of digital businesses.

The infrastructure required to support these ambitions extends beyond connectivity. Datacentres, cloud platforms, cyber security capabilities and access to advanced computing resources will all play a role in enabling organisations to develop and operate increasingly sophisticated digital services.

Sovereign infrastructure and regional competitiveness

For Qatar, expanding domestic datacentre capacity also has implications for data sovereignty and resilience.

Hosting workloads within national borders can help organisations meet data residency and regulatory requirements, particularly in sensitive sectors such as government, financial services and healthcare. It also gives local businesses and developers access to computing resources closer to their customers.

The ability to establish primary and disaster recovery environments across separate in-country facilities is another consideration for organisations seeking to strengthen business continuity and operational resilience.

These requirements are becoming more significant as AI adoption increases the volume and sensitivity of data being processed by organisations. Qatar is also seeking to position itself within a competitive regional digital infrastructure market, where governments and technology companies are investing heavily in hyperscale facilities, cloud platforms and AI computing capacity.

  • Qatar launches Qai to accelerate national and regional AI ambitions: State-backed company Qai aims to build secure AI infrastructure and position Qatar as a leading Gulf innovation hub.
  • MWC25 Doha debut marks a new chapter for MENA mobile innovation: GSMA’s Jawad Jalal Abbassi outlines how Qatar’s first Mobile World Congress will accelerate digital transformation, 5G adoption and AI integration across the region.
summary:
Syntys has begun construction on a 20MW (megawatt) datacentre in Qatar, part of the broader expansion of digital infrastructure in the country as demand for cloud computing, artificial intelligence (AI) and high-performance computing (HPC) rises across the Middle East.

The investment comes as Qatar seeks to strengthen its position as a regional technology hub, with digital infrastructure becoming an increasingly important part of its economic diversification and national development strategy.

The development also follows MWC26 Doha, which brought together more than 10,000 participants from 100 countries on 8 to 10 November. The event provided a platform for government leaders, telecommunications operators and technology companies to discuss the future of AI, next-generation connectivity and digital economies. 

For Qatar, the discussions at MWC Doha highlighted the importance of moving beyond technology adoption towards building the infrastructure, capabilities and partnerships required to support a more advanced digital economy.

Expanding Qatar’s datacentre ecosystem

The new Syntys facility forms part of the company’s strategy to expand its Qatar operations through a combination of acquisitions and new developments.

Earlier this year, Syntys acquired QData QFZ LLC, adding two operational, Tier III-compliant, carrier-neutral datacentre facilities to its portfolio. With the latest development, the company now owns and operates four campuses in Qatar, allowing customers to establish primary and disaster recovery environments across separate locations within the country.

The new facility is being developed on an existing Syntys campus, where power infrastructure, fibre connectivity and an established operations team are already in place. This is intended to accelerate the delivery of additional capacity while building on existing operational capabilities.

Designed to be Tier III-compliant, the facility will accommodate different rack densities, including higher-density configurations required for GPU-accelerated AI and HPC workloads.

As organisations move AI applications from experimentation into production, the underlying infrastructure requirements are changing.

title: AI agents bring down wind farm within two hours
raw_text:
Artificial intelligence (AI) agents can hack into wind farms, erase the memory of electronic controllers and cut off their electricity production capability in under two hours.

Research to be unveiled next week gives new urgency to calls for organisations to properly secure the networks used to manage critical physical infrastructure.

The warning follows a wave of attacks on refrigeration systems used by retailers across Europe, meat processors in the UK and a French blood bank.

According to “red team” reports from penetration testing company Shinobi Security, two off-the-shelf large language models (LLMs) were able to stop six turbines delivering nearly 10MW (megawatts) of power in a replicated wind farm, starting with “nothing but a set of VPN credentials”.

No specialist knowledge needed

The company’s head of research, David Mound, told Computer Weekly that the experiment shows that hackers no longer need specialist knowledge to attack devices used to control physical infrastructure – known as operational technology (OT).

He said the research showed that attackers could use an LLM to launch a successful attack without having detailed knowledge of how wind farms work.

“Even if you are not a seasoned OT red teamer or penetration tester, a normal attacker is able to amplify their capability by using and exploiting large language models. Even LLMs on their own are more than capable of penetrating and exploiting these environments,” he said.

Mound built a test rig from the same components used in a wind farm that was attacked by suspected Russian hackers in Poland in December 2025.

Poland’s Computer Emergency Response Team (CERT) published a detailed report on the incident, allowing Mound and his co-researchers to build a rig that mimicked the operation of a real wind farm.

The rig used the same networking devices and a Siemens controller to replicate the farm’s connection to the electricity grid. It was combined with simulations of Scada (supervisory control and data acquisition) and HMI (human-machine interface) controllers to mimic the operation of the wind turbines.

Moonshot and Claude

Mound said it was important to make the rig as true to life as possible to ensure that the AI agents believed they were acting in a real environment, as the experiment showed they would behave differently if they believed the test was a simulation.

The researchers tested Anthropic’s Claude LLM, along with Kimi, an open source, open-weight AI model supplied by Chinese AI startup Moonshot.

Both models were able to successfully shut down the wind farm in a fraction of the time taken by human attackers targeting similar plants in Poland.

Claude took 66 minutes to shut down the wind farm’s connection to the power grid, at a cost of $20 in tokens. Kimi took just under two hours to reach the same point at a cost of just $8.

“In the real Polish wind farm hack, the attackers were there for 11 days before they shut down the plant,” said Mound.

Misconfigured devices

The AI models followed a similar attack path to the real hack in Poland, exploiting misconfigured devices rather than attempting anything more sophisticated, such as hunting for zero-day vulnerabilities.

They were given credentials to access a VPN – information that could be found on the dark web – to make the initial access to the wind farm.

The models worked out how to access a control device with a web portal that had been set up with default credentials, and from there they were able to set up an encrypted tunnel and pivot into the rest of the network.

The AI systems worked out that the network contained an “historian” database, which, among other operational data, recorded the actions taken by controllers in response to different wind speeds over time.

“The speed and efficiency that the LLMs work at is a big concern. Domain-specific knowledge is no longer a barrier to entry for attacking these types of environments. Understanding that you are under attack within an hour is going to be very difficult”

David Mound, Shinobi Security

For the purpose of the experiment, the models were told not to do anything that would physically damage the infrastructure so that the experiment could be repeated.

“They were absolutely capable of turning off the power. And if it was a case of taking further malicious actions or deleting programs from the programmable logic controllers, they would have been more than capable of doing that themselves,” he said.

In a real-life attack, the LLMs could have been used by attackers to install ransomware on the control devices used in the wind farm, effectively shutting it down until the ransom was paid or until the wind farm could restore its systems from backups.

The turbine blades would have been protected from physical damage, as there are safety mechanisms in place to prevent them from spinning too quickly.

AI agent spoofed weather data

In an unexpected twist, one of the AI agents worked out how to spoof data from the weather station to make it appear that the wind was gusting, causing safety circuits to automatically shut down the turbines.

“It is incredible for an LLM to come up with that method of stopping the power because the main goal was to stop the power being placed on the grid,” he said.

One model also threatened to “drop the safety theatre” and take further destructive action if the researchers confirmed its hunch that the wind farm rig was a simulation, rather than a real wind farm.

When the Polish wind farm was attacked in December 2025, operators became aware that the plant had been attacked before there was a major incident. But a similar AI-driven attack would leave them with less time to react.

“The speed and efficiency that the LLMs work at is a big concern. Domain-specific knowledge is no longer a barrier to entry for attacking these types of environments,” said Mound. “Understanding that you are under attack within an hour is going to be very difficult.”

Getting basic security right

Protecting wind farms is a matter of getting the basics right, ensuring that network devices are not misconfigured and are not set to default passwords, said Mound.

It is also clear that information not generally regarded as sensitive for security purposes, such as records in the historian database, can be extremely useful for an LLM attacker. For example, it can use the information to work out that it has accessed a wind farm and how the wind farm operates.

“Those areas within a network where you have knowledge stores that you might not have thought had high value before now have much greater value when it comes to delivering context to an LLM,” he said.

Last week, Richard Horne, chief executive officer of the National Cyber Security Centre (NCSC), urged organisations to ensure that control devices were patched and updated, in the wake of the hacking attacks on supermarket fridges.

“Large businesses will have a large amount of operational technology, whether it’s manufacturing lines, heating controls, or building management systems,” he said. “All organisations need to be looking for them and addressing both the connectivity and the configuration of those devices.”

David Mound will be presenting his research at the Sans CyberThreat Summit on 16 November.

How AI agents closed down a wind farm

  1. VPN into the perimeter with the issued credentials.
  2. Factory default credentials used on the boundary controller.
  3. Enabled SSH on that controller and used it as a pivot to enumerate the OT segment reliably.
  4. Unauthenticated access control failure on an online code repository, Gitea, gave access to the site’s entire engineering document store, including the grid interface notes and the Scada account.
  5. The documents identified the substation controller with an open interface. A single command allowed the power breaker to be turned on.

 Source: Shinobi Security

title: Why the use of AI by the UK’s intelligence services needs independent oversight
raw_text:
Governments increasingly declare they are keen to regulate risky uses of artificial intelligence, yet they say little about how they will regulate their own AI tools. Some of the most secretive parts of the state - intelligence agencies - are actively using AI. We must urgently regulate spies' use of this incredibly powerful and potentially problematic technology.

Intelligence agencies across the world are utilising rapidly advancing AI tools to gather and process more data about more people than ever before. What makes these agencies’ use of advanced processing particularly dangerous, amidst the variety of government uses of AI, is that it is done in secret.

Bringing this conduct to light too often requires heavy lifting. At Privacy International, where I work, we’ve had to litigate repeatedly for transparency and surveillance safeguards in the UK and around the world. We’ve had to force governments to protect our human rights. We’re doing so right now in the case of secret orders reportedly issued to Apple to undermine the security of their iCloud storage. 

In our brave new world of rapidly evolving technology, each time a new, increasingly intrusive surveillance technique is revealed, we force the question: what specific safeguards should have been applied before governments grabbed the latest innovations and exceeded their powers?

Mass surveillance

We are at such a moment again. We’ve been tracking, as best we can, how intelligence agencies around the world are using advanced AI tools. For instance, during Anthropic’s conflict with the US Department of Defence in January 2026, the Pentagon reportedly wanted to use Anthropic’s technology to assist with “the collection and analysis of unclassified, commercial bulk data on Americans, such as geolocation and web browsing data.” Anthropic more recently revealed that actors in China, Iran and Mali were using their tools for mass surveillance and targeted cyber attacks.

We know UK intelligence agencies have the capacity to use advanced AI, including through a variety of contracts with US tech firms like Amazon that provide such tools.

In our research we’ve documented the use of AI tools that seem to make the previously impossible possible. This includes the sifting and understanding of vast amounts of data, including the results of mass surveillance. As the former heads of MI6 and the CIA stated together, AI tools assist with “identifying key information in a sea of data”. We’ve also found examples of these tools purportedly assisting governments to assign human sentiment and detect relationships, predict future human activity, conduct profiling and even identify targets in war.

Constraining this conduct needn’t be so challenging. While it is often said that the law lags behind innovation, this should never be true when complying with human rights and constitutional protections. Governments have a duty to ensure only lawful use of their powers. Oversight bodies, parliaments and legislatures should hold intelligence agencies to account. This is how the rule of law is supposed to work.

And yet we have mostly silence from the British state.

Deploying these techniques in secret robs those of us outside the agencies of meaningful participation in the debate about the risks to human rights that AI-enabled surveillance and intelligence gathering poses.

And in that darkness we also miss learning from errors and abuses. Last year the Guardian, +972 Magazine and Local Call reported that the Israeli military intelligence agency was training a large language model using millions of intercepted daily communications by Palestinians in the West Bank. Bloomberg recently reported that the over-reliance on AI tools may have led in part to the US forces’ missile strike on a school in Iran, killing 123 children. 

It need not be this way. Fortunately, many countries already have legal regimes governing intelligence gathering and use with attendant oversight bodies. Those laws need tightening, updating, and strengthening. Oversight bodies must be empowered with both the resources and technical expertise to grapple with advancing AI.

We all need to be a part of a conversation about how powerful we want the state to become through the use of AI. And we cannot afford for this conversation to be behind closed doors or for it to come too late.

Caroline Wilson Palow is Legal Director and General Counsel of Privacy International

Do they have what it takes to oversee the intelligence community?

Investigatory powers: Guidelines for police and spies could also help businesses with AI - Computer Weekly talks to Muffy Calder, technology advisor to the UK’s investigatory powers commissioner, about privacy, intrusion and artificial intelligence

title: Third Post Office Capture conviction referral adds to ‘growing body of evidence’
raw_text:
A third subpostmaster conviction based on evidence from the Post Office’s faulty Capture system has been referred to the Court of Appeal.

The Criminal Cases Review Commission (CCRC) deems the conviction of former Dudley subpostmaster Narinder Aujla, now 61, a possible miscarriage of justice.

Aujla was convicted of theft at Wolverhampton Crown Court in 1998, after losses of £10,000 appeared in his Capture-based accounts. He was sentenced to four months in prison and had to repay the shortfall on release.

After the Capture software was installed in the 1990s, Aujla began seeing discrepancies on the balance sheets, which he could not explain.

He is the third former Capture user to have a case referred. The conviction of former subpostmaster Steve Marston, who was a subpostmaster in Bury, Lancashire, in 1997, was referred by the CCRC for appeal in March, while the appeal against a 1998 conviction of Patricia Owen, who died in 2003, was the first Capture case to be referred to the Court of Appeal. These appeals are due to be heard in the Court of Appeal in January.

Aujla’s story is one heard many times before. He had been balancing the books by adding his own money, and when this became impossible, he was advised by the Post Office helpline to “roll the losses over” to the next week, but each time he did this, the total loss increased. 

It is the fourth case referred in relation to a system used before the controversial Horizon software, which caused hundreds of miscarriages of justice. As well as the three Capture-based referrals, there is one more based on a prosecution of a user of a system known as APT/APS.

• Read more: Post Office Horizon scandal explained – everything you need to know •

The Criminal Cases Review Commission is currently reviewing 12 Capture-based prosecutions. Unlike convictions based on the Horizon system, which were overturned en masse through legislation, those based on Capture have to go through the CCRC.

Capture, which predates Fujitsu’s Horizon system, was used in Post Office branches in the 1990s to replace paper-based accounting. As with the controversial Horizon system at the centre of the Post Office scandal, which saw subpostmasters blamed for unexplained losses, some Capture users were prosecuted for financial crimes.

The controversy over Capture emerged in January 2024, after ITV drama Mr Bates vs the Post Office told the stories of subpostmasters who had suffered at the hands of the Horizon system.

In the same month, Kevan Jones, an MP at the time who now sits in the House of Lords, highlighted evidence of injustices triggered by Capture losses.

This led to a campaign and, by December 2024, the government promised financial redress and justice for subpostmasters affected by Capture problems. This followed an independent investigation by forensic experts at Kroll, which found there was a “reasonable likelihood” the Post Office Capture software caused accounting losses.

Body of evidence

CCRC chair Vera Baird KC said: “We have had a number of pre-Horizon cases – that is those which relate to accounting systems placed in branches by the Post Office prior to the now notoriously defective Horizon one – which it seems might similarly have generated false losses later blamed on Post Office staff.  

“Capture is one of those earlier systems, and this is now the third Capture-related conviction we have referred to the Court of Appeal, adding to a growing body of evidence that Capture was in that category of ‘guilty’ Post Office software systems which have generated so much wrong and suffering for hardworking subpostmasters.”

She added: “In Mr Aujla’s case, the new evidence, considered alongside the findings of the independent reports into Capture, gives rise to a real possibility that the Court of Appeal will conclude that his prosecution was an abuse of process. We remain committed to identifying and reviewing cases where convictions may have been affected by unreliable Post Office accounting systems. 

“Cases of this kind also serve as a reminder of the profound personal impact that criminal convictions can have. For those affected, the consequences have often extended far beyond the courtroom, affecting their livelihoods, finances, reputations and family lives for many years.”

The government recently announced an investigation of pre-Horizon systems and their impact on subpostmaster users. While this will not include Capture, which has already been proven to be faulty, it will look at APT/APS, ECCO+, ALPS, ESNS and potentially others.

Timeline of how Capture controversy unravelled since Horizon scandal dramatisation

  • Jan 2024: MP demands answers from government minister over second faulty Post Office IT system.
  • Feb 2024: More than 1,000 subpostmasters could have used second faulty Post Office system.
  • Feb 2024: Government won’t rush to include Post Office Capture convictions in overturning legislation.
  • Feb 2024: Post Office CEO’s claim to be ‘working hard’ on Capture investigation in doubt.
  • Mar 2024: Controversial Post Office Capture software was completely rewritten in 1994.
  • Mar 2024: Post Office Capture users’ campaign for justice gathers pace.
  • Apr 2024: Expert investigating Capture system refuses to meet ‘untrustworthy’ Post Office.
  • May 2024: Government appoints investigators to analyse Post Office Capture software used before Horizon.
  • May 2024: Mystery Post Office software developer revealed in 1995 Horizon project document.
  • June 2024: Post Office Capture software training deficit echoes systemic Horizon problems.
  • Sept 2024: More parallels between Post Office Capture and Horizon scandal revealed.
  • Sept 2024: Investigation finds 'reasonable likelihood' Post Office Capture software caused accounting losses.
  • Oct 2024: Late evidence in Post Office Capture investigation could not be reviewed.
  • Oct 2024: Review of late evidence doesn’t change Post Office Capture system report.
  • Oct 2024: Government ‘urged’ to overturn all convictions based on Post Office Capture.
  • Nov 2024: Convictions of Post Office Capture system users to be reviewed by statutory body.
  • Dec 2024: Government promises redress and justice to Post Office Capture users.
  • Jan 2025: Former subpostmasters invited to take part in Post Office Capture compensation scheme development.
  • Feb 2025: CCRC reviewing 17 Post Office convictions with potential Capture software involvement.
  • April 2025: Post Office Capture and Ecco+ users asked to make contact with Scottish statutory body.
  • July 2025: First Post Office Capture conviction referred to Court of Appeal.
  • Sept 2025: Post Office Capture appeals slowed by poor records.
  • Oct 2025: CCRC formally sends Post Office Capture referral to Court of Appeal.
  • Oct 2025: Government awards Post Office £2m contract to search for its own Capture records.
  • Oct 2025: Post Office Capture redress scheme ‘went down like lead balloon’ and is ‘discriminatory’.
  • Nov 2025: Unearthed report reveals source of Post Office’s tenuous Capture sales pitch.
  • January 2026: History repeats itself in Post Office Capture redress scheme with low-ball offers made.
  • February 2026: Minister responds to criticism of Post Office Capture redress scheme.
  • March 2026: Report from MPs warns of unknown number of unsafe subpostmasters convictions based on multiple pre-Horizon systems.
  • November 2026: Conviction of 30 years has been referred to the Court of Appeal by the Criminal Cases Review Commission.

title: Bug-hunting time cut dramatically with AI, says Forescout
raw_text:
Artificial intelligence (AI) is making faster and easier discovery of vulnerabilities in code that is common in critical infrastructure, according to findings from Forescout’s research arm Vedere Labs.

The Forescout report, Finding critical infrastructure bugs with off-the-shelf AI looked at how security researchers and attackers can use generally available AI models and a limited budget to find vulnerabilities in both open source software and proprietary “binaries”, which are executable computer files.

The Vedere researchers built an AI vulnerability “research harness” – software infrastructure around a large language model (LLM) – and applied it to 10 TCP/IP stacks, including seven they had analysed in 2020-21, in a project dubbed Memoria.

Daniel dos Santos, vice-president of research at Forescout, based in Eindhoven in the Netherlands, said: “AI did not eliminate the need for expert vulnerability researchers, but it dramatically compressed the work.

“With access to an effective AI-assisted workflow, vulnerabilities in complex embedded software can be found much faster and at a fraction of the cost by security researchers and attackers alike.

“Our research demonstrates that AI is changing the economics of vulnerability discovery and accelerating the pace at which security teams need to identify, prioritise and mitigate cyber risk. This is especially impactful for critical infrastructure, where legacy and difficult-to-patch devices may remain in service for years.”

The threats converging on operational technology and IT was a theme of the research as presented to a small group of journalists in London.

The supplier’s cyber threat landscape findings for the UK, presented by Dos Santos at the same event, stated that 108 threat actors have targeted the UK in 2026. Most were cyber criminals (55%), then state-sponsored actors (33%), then hacktivists (12%).

There were 227 hacktivist attack claims against the UK between 1 January and 30 September, according to Vedere’s research team. This represents a 337% increase over the 52 claims observed in all of 2025 – 60% were claimed by two active pro-Russian groups, NoName057 (16) and the Z Pentest Alliance.

Some 29% of the attackers tracked by Forescout are from Russia, 20% in China, 6% in Iran, 5% in North Korea, and the remaining 40% come from other countries.

Forescout’s research team said: “We continue to observe hacktivist groups targeting British government institutions, public services and organisations perceived as strategically important due to the UK’s geopolitical role and support for international allies.”

With respect to the AI-assisted approach used for their most recent research project, the researchers said their results have shown that AI reduced analysis time from approximately nine months to 90 hours. It uncovered 99 vulnerabilities, including 66 previously unknown.

Some 52% of the new bugs were rated as high or critical severity. The cost of the automated analysis was $935, averaging just $2.58 per finding.

TCP/IP stacks are embedded in products used used in OT, internet of things (IoT), medical devices, network equipment, and other systems that are both physical and cyber.

The same underlying software can be used across products from many and varied manufacturers, so a single vulnerability can create risk across a broad technology supply chain, the researchers said.

Barry Mainz, CEO at Forescout, said: “The speed of vulnerability discovery is increasing with AI, but the reality for asset owners and operators has not changed. Organisations still have legacy systems, operational requirements and devices that can’t easily be patched or simply taken offline. Containing risk, rather than patching, must be the priority.”

title: Brian Leveson on AI, candour and investigatory powers
raw_text:
The investigatory powers commissioner, Lord Brian Leveson, relies on the security and intelligence services, police and other government agencies being open and honest.

Leveson leads the body that oversees the use of covert investigatory powers for 600 public authorities, including the UK’s intelligence agencies, law enforcement, police, councils and prisons.

In an interview with Computer Weekly, the former senior judge explains how the oversight body is preparing for the impact of artificial intelligence (AI) on intelligence gathering and policing, and how he relies on the bodies he oversees to be candid when they make mistakes.

Leveson’s job is to ensure that government agencies use intrusive powers – which range from accessing the communications data from phones to hacking into criminal communications networks and the bulk surveillance of internet traffic – in a lawful, proportionate way.

The Investigatory Powers Commissioner’s Office (IPCO) employs 150 people, including officers who authorise requests for communications data from law enforcement and other government bodies, judicial commissioners, inspectors, lawyers and support staff – a relatively small team for a huge task.

We can’t look at everything

“We can’t look at everything, and we don’t look at everything – and we don’t want to. Because if we were looking at more, we would be taking important frontline workers [in the bodies that fall under IPCO’s remit] off looking at what might happen tomorrow to what happened yesterday,” he tells Computer Weekly.

Leveson was appointed as the UK’s second investigatory powers commissioner in October 2019, and over the past eight-and-a-half years, he has built up good personal relationships with the heads of MI5, GCHQ, MI6 and other government bodies he oversees.

“We get on, and they know they can phone me, and they occasionally do just that,” he says.

The duty of candour

Leveson relies on those organisations to draw his attention to any problems or failure to comply with the Investigatory Powers Act, its accompanying codes of practice and other relevant laws.

His oversight is backed by a regime of on-the-spot inspections – more than 400 in 2025 – which include taking a random sample of surveillance authorisations, examining records and focusing on activities where risks could arise.

“When I was a judge, if the security services said something, then I would accept it. I think the court is going to be far more reluctant to accept, without evidential proof, things said in the future”

Brian Leveson, IPCO

“The trouble is always going to come where somebody does something wrong and does not fess up, and they do occasionally do that,” says Leveson.

That happened spectacularly when MI5 lied to two courts and misled Leveson over its handling of Agent X, a violent neo-Nazi who coercively controlled and attacked his partner.

MI5 falsely maintained to Leveson and the courts that it had stuck to its core secrecy obligations – to neither confirm nor deny the agent’s identity – when it had already disclosed that information to the BBC.

When BBC journalist Daniel De Simone produced a recording of his conversation with an MI5 officer proving that the Secret Service had lied, there were reverberations around the intelligence community.

Have lessons been learned?

“I think that everybody learns from disasters, and this, for MI5, has been a very serious matter. But I believe they have learned and I believe they have got the message,” he says.

Courts will be less willing in future, he suggests, to take what MI5 says at face value without supporting evidence.

“When I was a judge, if the security services said something, then I would accept it. I think the court is going to be far more reluctant to accept, without evidential proof, things said in the future.”

Other examples of lack of candour have come to light through cases brought by journalists in Northern Ireland in the Investigatory Powers Tribunal after they were unlawfully placed under surveillance.

Troubles in Northern Ireland

IPCO missed the existence of an unlawful Directed Surveillance Authorisation taken out against journalists Barry McCaffrey and Trevor Birney during their inspection of the Police Service of Northern Ireland (PSNI) in 2019. What went wrong?

“The weakness is that they [PSNI] were supposed to tell us about directed surveillance of journalists and they didn’t. How that came about, I don’t know. We can’t look at everything … but that is why I must rely on them, and they know that,” Leveson tells Computer Weekly.

The incident dates back to a difficult time in the politics of Northern Ireland, he says. But the PSNI’s chief constable, Jon Boutcher, who took over in 2023, “is absolutely on top of making sure we see what we should see”.

Nevertheless, says Leveson, there was a failing. “There is no doubt the Northern Irish know what I think about it, [just] as the security services know what I think,” he tells Computer Weekly.

Artificial intelligence offers new capabilities

AI is giving intelligence and law enforcement agencies new capabilities, offering the potential to scan huge volumes of data to find relevant information quickly.

IPCO is building an “evidence-based picture” of how government bodies may use AI to exercise covert powers, and how IPCO can exercise its oversight in an age of machine learning and large language models.

Leveson has no immediate plans for IPCO to use AI in its oversight work, but is working with its Technical Advisory Panel, led by Dame Muffy Calder, a distinguished academic at Glasgow University, to ensure its systems are ready for AI when the time comes.

One area of interest for Leveson is in finding out how AI could help him identify priority cases for inspectors to review. “I would love a mechanism to find the nuggets, the things that I should be looking at, rather than just having it randomly selected,” he says.

How AI could be used in police and intelligence

AI has the potential to gather and analyse vast quantities of public and private data, track and predict people’s movements, map relationships and identify intelligence targets.

A report published by GCHQ in February 2025 suggested that AI could be used to identify potential grooming behaviour by analysing the contents of intercepted messages and images.

It could also be used to map organised crime groups, analyse financial transactions, track deliveries of illicit cargo and identify state-backed disinformation campaigns.

“AI will be vital to our ability to deal with the ever-increasing volume and complexity of data, and to develop the capabilities needed to defend against AI-enabled threats by malicious actors,” the report said.

There is little regulation over the use of AI in the UK, and it carries risks, such as the tendency to hallucinate or make mistakes. Its ability to make predictions and inferences about people by pulling together large amounts of data gives it intrusive capabilities.

Another question is whether data used to train AI can ever be deleted if intelligence agencies decide it is no longer proportionate to keep the information in their files.

Last year, IPCO’s Technical Advisory Panel published a framework – the AI Proportionality Assessment Aid – to help government agencies think about whether their use of AI is proportionate and minimises invasion of privacy.

Leveson sees AI’s ability to analyse volumes of data in ways that go beyond human capabilities as an asset that could lead to better policing and better performance by the intelligence services. But he has caveats.

“First of all, what is going on in the black box? What decisions are being made, what biases are being perhaps inadvertently built in and how can I detect them? And how can I find a mechanism to ensure that compliance works in the AI as well?” he asks.

Compliance by design

Leveson has challenged agencies that are building AI tools to build in “compliance by design” so that inspectors have a mechanism to identify what material they should be looking at to gain effective oversight.

If an AI system makes an incorrect decision that has a negative impact on an individual, that would have to be reported to IPCO. If it’s a serious error, Leveson would write to the individual, informing them of their right to seek redress through the Investigatory Powers Tribunal.

“It’s a rather oblique letter because you can’t tell them exactly what has happened,” he tells Computer Weekly. But he says people can go to the tribunal without having a lawyer, and the tribunal can investigate errors, provide redress and potentially award compensation.

The Investigatory Powers Act, introduced in 2016 in the aftermath of the Edward Snowden revelations, put the UK’s sophisticated surveillance capabilities on a solid statutory footing for the first time, avowing the existence of formerly secret capabilities.

Leveson is nevertheless constrained over the issues he can talk about publicly, including the widely reported case of the Home Office issuing a technical capability notice to Apple to allow UK agencies access to end-to-end encrypted data stored on the Apple iCloud under warrant.

The case sparked a diplomatic row between the UK and the US, with US president Donald Trump and former US director of national intelligence Tulsi Gabbard intervening over the case, which is still playing out in the Investigatory Powers Tribunal.

Leveson says private sector companies, such as Meta and Google, know more about individuals than the state does and, like the intelligence services of hostile states, have fewer constraints over how they use that data than UK government agencies.

To encrypt or not to encrypt?

The debate over end-to-end encryption is a fraught one. Police and intelligence services are pushing for access to the content of encrypted messages through technologies such as client-side scanning, while cryptography experts warn that undermining end-to-end encryption will put the public at greater risk of cyber attacks from criminals and hostile states.

Where does the balance lie? Leveson suggests it’s ultimately a matter for civil society, Parliament and ministers.

“There ought to be some mechanism that can pick up threats to our national security. Then you have to decide what the mechanism is and what protections it requires,” he says.

“I won’t give a view,” he adds. “But I would ask you to decide: Is it sensible that terrorists can communicate entirely on an end-to-end encrypted basis without giving us a chance of identifying them?”
