title: Last orders ‘very soon’ for Fujitsu’s Post Office scandal financial contribution
raw_text:
Fujitsu’s excuse for holding back its contribution to the costs of the Post Office scandal could be about to expire, along with its ineffective moratorium on bidding for government contracts.

Fujitsu has clung to the excuse that it will pay what it owes after the publication of the final Post Office scandal public inquiry report and it has stuck to its word on that. In contrast, while it also promised not to bid for government contracts until the inquiry reported, caveats have meant it has been business as usual.

According to the Law Gazette, Emma Price, counsel to the Post Office Horizon IT Inquiry, said the report’s final volumes are in the “final writing stages” and will be published ‘very soon”.

Fujitsu made two significant commitments in the aftermath of ITV’s drama in January 2024 about the scandal. It declared that it had a moral duty to pay towards the cost of the scandal and promised not to bid for government contracts.

On holding back its contribution, a Fujitsu spokesperson said: “We believe it is the right thing to do for Fujitsu to contribute to compensation and, as we have consistently stated, this will be agreed with government after Wyn Williams has published the findings of his inquiry. Our conversations with government regarding our contribution are ongoing.”

Fujitsu has been less rigid on its self-imposed ban on bidding for government project. In April 2024, just a couple of months after the supplier banned itself from bidding for government contracts, Computer Weekly reported that the company’s then public sector boss was instructing staff on how to get around the self-imposed ban.

Read more: Post Office Horizon scandal explained: Everything you need to know.

Fujitsu was not held back by its ban. According to market watcher Tussell, between May 2024 and April 2025, Fujitsu made sales worth £453m to the UK public sector – more than in the previous 12 months – and it has continued to do so. Just this past week, Fujitsu has won the contract to support the Emergency Alerts Services, which will initially cost £9m for three years, with an option to extend by 12 more months.

Also this week, the Post Office announced another extension to its controversial contract with Fujitsu. It said this is the last short contract it will have with Fujitsu for Horizon, but with the previous 12-month contract costing £40m, this extension – likely six months – could cost £20m. This will be the third since the scandal became wide public knowledge after the TV drama in January 2024.

Fujitsu has won hundreds of millions of pounds worth of government contracts with organisations such as HMRC, the Met Police and the Post Office since it imposed its bidding ban. In the summer, Fujitsu was confirmed as a supplier on four government procurement frameworks by the Government Commercial Agency (GCA), worth more than £54bn in total.

Meanwhile, the cost of the scandal for UK taxpayers is now counted in billions of pounds.

Peer James Arbuthnot, who has campaigned alongside subpostmasters for nearly two decades, said: “The government is behaving as though the country is over a barrel to Fujitsu, because nobody else could do the work they do. I very much doubt that this is true.

“Even if it were true, we as a country should not be doing business with a company that colludes in such terrible miscarriages of justice. By doing so we are sending the message that ethics don’t matter. This is not who we are, and the government needs to get a grip of this matter that is fundamental to our character.”

The getaway driver

Fujitsu’s Horizon software was at the centre of the scandal, with subpostmasters blamed and punished for accounting shortfalls caused by software errors. It is today widely regarded as one of the biggest miscarriages of justice in history, with around a thousand people wrongly convicted of crimes, with many sent to prison, and thousands more having their lives turned over through financial hardship.

Fujitsu knew the system had errors that could cause unexplained losses, but gave evidence in court during prosecutions of subpostmasters claiming Horizon was robust and could not have caused the shortfalls that the subpostmasters were being blamed for.

When forced, Fujitsu’s then European boss, Paul Patterson, admitted at a Post Office Horizon scandal public inquiry hearing in 2024 that the IT company missed an opportunity to take action and prevent subpostmasters from being convicted.

Read more: Fujitsu’s role in the Post Office scandal: Everything you need to know.

Despite requests for up-front contributions, Fujitsu is playing a waiting game. The public inquiry’s first report was played down by a senior Fujitsu executive in an internal meeting last year.

In October 2025, after the inquiry chair published its first report, which linked Fujitsu’s software problems to 13 suicides, a recording heard by Computer Weekly revealed that a senior executive at the supplier said the report “was not that bad”. He has since left the supplier.

Read more about the Post Office scandal public inquiry

  • Round-up of phase two: Post Office scandal – ‘cock-up or cook-up’?
  • Round-up of phase three: Post Office scandal – cover-up a ‘dark chapter’ in government, corporate and legal history.
  • Round-up of phase four: Post Office scandal: Phase four’s rogues’ gallery.
  • Round-up of the combined phases five and six: Post Office scandal: Phases 5 and 6 had islands of conscientiousness in great depths of neglect.
  • Round up of phase seven: Post Office scandal: Inquiry’s final phase exposes dysfunction past and present.

The first report, which was published in July 2025, was described as “profoundly disturbing” by the Post Office Horizon scandal public inquiry chair, Wyn Williams. It focused on the human impact of the scandal, which came in phase one of the inquiry.

When the second part of the public inquiry report is published next year, Fujitsu will be exposed to huge public pressure. The second, more substantial report will cover the remaining six phases of the inquiry. Pertinent to Fujitsu’s role, the remaining phases covered issues including the Horizon IT system’s history, its operation, and legal actions against subpostmasters.

Sir Alan Bates, the former subpostmaster who led the fight against the Post Office and government which led to the public inquiry, said: “I would like to think the report when published will stop people hiding behind the inquiry, but it won’t because everyone will say, ‘We need months to read and review it.’ It’s just the next stage really, the next step on the way to the Metropolitan Police investigation report.”

The Post Office scandal was first exposed by Computer Weekly in 2009, revealing the stories of seven subpostmasters, including Bates, and the problems they suffered due to Horizon accounting software.

summary:
Fujitsu’s excuse for holding back its contribution to the costs of the Post Office scandal could be about to expire, along with its ineffective moratorium on bidding for government contracts.

Fujitsu has clung to the excuse that it will pay what it owes after the publication of the final Post Office scandal public inquiry report and it has stuck to its word on that. In contrast, while it also promised not to bid for government contracts until the inquiry reported, caveats have meant it has been business as usual.

According to the Law Gazette, Emma Price, counsel to the Post Office Horizon IT Inquiry, said the report’s final volumes are in the “final writing stages” and will be published ‘very soon”.

Fujitsu made two significant commitments in the aftermath of ITV’s drama in January 2024 about the scandal. It declared that it had a moral duty to pay towards the cost of the scandal and promised not to bid for government contracts.

On holding back its contribution, a Fujitsu spokesperson said: “We believe it is the right thing to do for Fujitsu to contribute to compensation and, as we have consistently stated, this will be agreed with government after Wyn Williams has published the findings of his inquiry. Our conversations with government regarding our contribution are ongoing.”

Fujitsu has been less rigid on its self-imposed ban on bidding for government project.

title: The ethics of using books to train AI
raw_text:
Training artificial intelligence (AI) systems such as ChatGPT and Claude requires vast amounts of data. It is generally acknowledged that the better the data, the better the AI becomes. In the past couple of years, we have seen AI companies gain agreements with various organisations to access their data. However, some AI companies have been exploring alternative data sources.

In January 2026, it was revealed that Claude creator Anthropic had been acquiring secondhand books and scanning them at an industrial scale to train its AI system. A side-effect of this industrial-scale digitisation was that the books were destroyed in the process.

In August 2026, it was reported that a shipment of rare books was tracked to an Amazon AI training facility.

“Disclosures in US legal proceedings demonstrate that staff within these companies understood the seriousness of using copyright-protected content without permission,” says Catriona MacLeod Stevenson, general counsel and deputy CEO of the Publisher’s Association.

“An internal memo released in the New York Times’ lawsuit against OpenAI and Microsoft records a Microsoft executive describing the development of large language models as ‘an astonishing theft of unprecedented proportions’,” she adds.

It is also worth noting that the destroyed books were not just mass-produced paperbacks. Some were antique editions, which were rare and unavailable elsewhere.

“It is incredibly easy for AI companies to scan books. It’s so trivial, and you can do it at scale,” says Patrick Smith, field chief technology officer (CTO) at Pure Storage. “Doing it at scale is the reason the books are destroyed, because they need to cut the spine off so that they can feed it through scanning machines at incredible speed. Nothing in the world of AI training happens at small scale; it is a large-scale operation.”

Published books vs online text

Unlike online material, such as social media posts and blogs, books offer a higher quality of data. Books have been edited to a more stringent level than most online material, and usually someone has paid the author to publish them, so the grammar and punctuation are of a higher standard. Furthermore, books can articulate long-form arguments well, unlike online material, which is often shorter and more condensed.

“We’ve talked for so long about ‘garbage in garbage out (GIGO)’, and it remains true,” says Smith. “If AI models were trained on higher quality data, then you wouldn’t need so much of it. I’m not sure that AI models know what good looks like.”

By using books that were printed before 2022 (the year ChatGPT was launched), developers can be certain that generative AI was not used in the writing of the books. AI models lose accuracy after being recursively trained on data produced by other AI systems, as it can lead to a degenerative learning process and ultimately model collapse.

Copyright and licensing challenges

Authors and publishers have experienced multifarious challenges following the release of generative AI systems. There have been questions about the legality of AI tools being trained on copyrighted works and concerns that some AI systems can generate text in the style of specific authors.

In the US, there is the fair use doctrine (part of Section 107 of the 1976 Copyright Act), which permits limited use of copyrighted material, such as for converting physical media into digital files, without permission from the copyright holder. In the UK, Section 29 of the Copyright, Designs and Patents Act 1988 permits the conversion of physical media into digital, but only if it is for non-commercial purposes.

“UK copyright law provides specific ‘fair dealing’ exceptions, which are narrower and not interchangeable with US fair use,” says Stevenson. “Whether a particular use qualifies as a ‘fair dealing’ depends on the facts, including whether the amount taken was reasonable and appropriate. A use is unlikely to be fair if it substitutes for the original work and causes the copyright owner to lose revenue.”

It is worth noting that some books exist outside of copyright controls. For example, the copyright will have expired for some works (in the UK, this is usually 70 years following the author’s death) and some will have been published free of copyright limitations.

This has brought up the question of territorialism in copyright enforcement. If an AI system is trained in a country where it is permitted to use copyrighted material, what happens when that AI is deployed in regions that have much stricter copyright controls?

Territorial control in copyright was one of the core elements in the Getty Images vs Stability AI legal case.

“We all thought that this case was going to provide clarification in this area,” says Mark Deem, digital lawyer and founder of Fortiter. “Unfortunately, it didn’t, because on this specific point, they could not easily establish that the copying took place within the territorial limit of the UK, and the question was not finally resolved.”

The aforementioned regional challenges of AI and copyright licence agreements are similar to those experienced by the film industry. Since 1997, the film industry has used digital rights management to control the regionalisation approach to DVD and Blu-ray distribution around the world.

Does AI learning require content licensing regulation?

Given the copyright challenges of AI training, it raises the question of whether there needs to be a global consensus regarding the use of copyrighted material for the purposes of training AI. Just as the General Data Protection Regulation has become the de facto standard for data protection regulation, does the AI sector require a similar approach to regulation?

Some publishers have already agreed licensing agreements, whereby AI companies that agree to certain conditions can train AI on that publisher’s books, provided they and their authors are appropriately compensated for the use of their material.

“There is an emerging licensing market, which enables AI companies and rights holders to enter into licensing deals and agree on terms and remuneration about how the work is to be used,” says Ambre Morvan, senior public policy manager and contracts adviser for the Society of Authors.

In its drive to compete with other countries, the UK government published a paper outlining four proposals for copyright reform.

Two of the proposals suggested weakening copyright laws by providing exceptions for when works are used for the purpose of training AI systems. However, following a campaign by the creative industries, the government has since indicated it will no longer proceed with any proposals that would weaken the existing copyright framework.

“The law can never prescribe exactly where technology is developing and how it’s developing, but it can provide the appropriate guardrails for the way in which it is developed, and we need to be very careful that what we don’t allow the laxing of those guardrails to be dressed up as an opportunity to try to get better development of AI,” says Deem.

“It’s not the speed that is the issue at the moment, it’s making sure that the guardrails are there to make sure it develops in the right way, respectful of where society is at the moment, the rights people have within society at the moment and the potential damage it could do to the creative industries.”

The future of AI training

As an alternative to large-scale AI, small language models (SLMs) are being deployed for specific tasks, which therefore require far less data to be effective. However, small language models lack the multi-functionality of large language models (LLMs).

“Some organisations actually prefer, rather than large language models, small language models; models that are highly tuned for specific purposes,” says Smith. “They are trained on specific data for particular use cases, so it’s not a case of large language models or nothing.”

Nonetheless, there remains a need for an international regulatory framework for AI systems to ensure that they are trained and deployed appropriately and ethically. However, given current geopolitical tensions, any form of internationally agreed treaty seems unlikely.

Anthropic was approached for comment, but did not respond.

Training artificial intelligence (AI) systems such as ChatGPT and Claude requires vast amounts of data. It is generally acknowledged that the better the data, the better the AI becomes. In the past couple of years, we have seen AI companies gain agreements with various organisations to access their data. However, some AI companies have been exploring alternative data sources.

title: Google Cloud pins London outage on PLC misconfiguration
raw_text:
Google has traced the 20 October power failure that knocked out UK banks, courts and couriers to a programmable logic controller (PLC) that measured mains voltage on the wrong side of a circuit breaker – a single sensing error that stopped the site’s emergency generators from starting and let the UPS batteries run flat.

The outage began at about 06:53 BST, when an external underground cable fault knocked out the facility’s primary utility feed at the datacentre that hosts europe-west2-b, one of three availability zones in the London region.

The site should have ridden through the fault. Instead, its diesel generators never started, the static UPS batteries – designed to work for only about five minutes – drained, and the data halls lost power completely.

The reason the generators stayed silent lies with a maintenance decision made a week earlier. After a quarterly generator load test on 14 October, Google isolated the second mains feed for corrective repairs, leaving the site in what the report calls a “temporary single-feed (1N) bridged maintenance posture” rather than its usual dual-feed (2N) design.

When the remaining feed then failed, no live mains supply was left – and the controller that should have called the generators into action looked in the wrong place.

A PLC is a rugged industrial computer that runs simple control logic. When incoming voltage falls, it starts the generators. The flaw was in where it took its measurement.

The PLC’s undervoltage sensors were wired upstream of the isolated feed B breaker. That breaker was open, but the cable on the utility side of it stayed energised. Therefore, when feed A failed, the controller saw healthy voltage on the still-live feed B cable – a cable connected to nothing the building actually used – and concluded the mains was fine. No undervoltage was detected, so no start command was issued.

Google outage timeline

  • 14 October: A quarterly generator load test ends with the second mains feed (feed B) isolated for corrective repairs, dropping the site from dual-feed (2N) to a temporary single-feed (1N) maintenance posture.
  • 20 October, 06:53: An underground cable fault on the utility network knocks out feed A, the only active mains feed.
  • 07:00: The generators fail to start; the UPS batteries, designed to bridge roughly five minutes, drain, and the data halls lose power.
  • 07:04–07:08: Google monitoring detects the failure.
  • 07:09: Automated failover begins to europe-west2-a and europe-west2-c; capacity saturates and cross-zone API calls time out.
  • 07:54: Standby utility power is restored to the facility.
  • 08:20: Power returns to the data halls after engineers reset and test the generator controllers.
  • 08:40–08:50: Clusters and network devices return, and deliberately throttled storage recovery begins.
  • 11:45: Controlled re-admission of traffic to europe-west2-b begins.
  • 12:11: Platform services and APIs are fully available, though some virtual machines remain down.
  • 13:08: More than 99% of Compute Engine VMs are healthy, and Google marks the main impact resolved after six hours and eight minutes.
  • 15:03: Google posts its closure notice, though some downstream services, including Revolut, still report issues into the afternoon.

Google’s report calls it “a misconfiguration of the PLC logic that did not verify both an undervoltage condition and physical breaker position”.

In plain terms, the controller asked whether the street still had power, but not whether that power was still reaching the building – the electrical equivalent of checking the mains outside the house rather than the trip switch in your own fuse box.

The consequence was a zone-wide blackout and a cascade across the region.

Google lists more than 35 Google Cloud services affected in europe-west2. These included:

  • Core compute: Compute Engine, Kubernetes Engine, Cloud Run, App Engine;
  • Data platforms: BigQuery, Cloud SQL, Spanner, AlloyDB;
  • Storage: Cloud Storage, Persistent Disk;
  • Networking: Virtual Private Cloud, Cloud Load Balancing, Cloud NAT.

Downstream, the failure rippled through household names. Reports at the time named Lloyds, HSBC, Halifax and Revolut among the banks affected, alongside HM Courts & Tribunals Service video hearings, Royal Mail, parts of the NHS, and a string of retailers and delivery firms.

Technology suppliers including Stripe, Snowflake, MongoDB and JFrog also reported knock-on problems, while the disruption later prompted MPs to ask finance regulators how they would handle future concentration risk in Google Cloud.

With the zone dark, automated failover shifted workloads to the two surviving zones. The sudden influx of redirected compute, database failovers and cross-zone traffic saturated available capacity, produced queue backlogs, delayed failovers, and created intermittent HTTP 500 and 503 errors across the wider London region.

Google has described this as a degraded state rather than a full regional control-plane outage, but multi-zonal and regional services still experienced elevated latency and application programming interface timeouts, while some customers in the untouched zones reported impact.

TL;DR

Google’s final incident report traces the 20 October outage of its London europe-west2 region to a programmable logic controller that watched mains voltage on the wrong side of a circuit breaker.

Because it saw a live cable, it never started the backup generators; the UPS batteries then ran out, and the resulting failover surge degraded the whole region for roughly six hours.

Google has outlined the fixes. It reconfigured and tested the PLC code and undervoltage logic so that generator startup now relies on actual busbar de-energisation – and breaker position – rather than upstream voltage readings, with validation taking place on 20 and 26 October.

It has begun to audit PLC configurations at other facilities with similar topologies, and has scheduled coordinated cable repairs, generator confidence load-transfer tests and full restoration of dual-feed utility configuration through November.

The incident carries a wider lesson for enterprise IT. Defence in depth – dual feeds, batteries and generators – was undone by one sensing error that only mattered because the site was already running in a degraded maintenance posture. Because Google operates a single UK cloud region, there was no regional failover to lean on, and the surviving zones, designed to absorb a lost zone’s traffic, saturated, which is why even customers that ran multi-zone architectures felt the impact.

The episode underlines the continuity lessons for IT leaders that follow any supposedly redundant cloud design, at a time when the cost and complexity of datacentre outages continues to climb.

title: MWC26 Doha: Qatar positions itself as a global technology hub
raw_text:
Qatar is looking to turn its growing investments in digital infrastructure, artificial intelligence and technology innovation into a platform for international growth, as the country seeks to establish itself as a regional technology hub and expand the global reach of its digital businesses.

The ambition was a key theme at MWC26 Doha, where government officials, telecommunications operators and technology leaders gathered to discuss the future of connectivity and the digital economy across the Middle East and North Africa (MENA).

Held in partnership with Qatar’s Ministry of Communications and Information Technology (MCIT), the second edition of MWC Doha at the Doha Exhibition and Convention Centre brought together the mobile industry and the International Telecommunication Union’s (ITU) Plenipotentiary Conference.

The event comes as mobile technology’s economic contribution across MENA continues to grow. According to the GSMA’s Mobile Economy MENA 2026 report, mobile technologies and services generated $380bn in economic value across the region in 2025, equivalent to 5.8% of regional GDP. This figure is forecast to reach $470bn by 2030.

For Qatar, the opportunity extends beyond expanding domestic connectivity. The country wants to develop an ecosystem that can produce and export digital services, software and technology solutions to international markets, while strengthening its position as a technology and innovation centre for the wider region.

From digital infrastructure to digital exports

During the event, officials from MCIT highlighted how the country’s National Digital Development Strategy is placing digital exports at the centre of its economic diversification ambitions.

The strategy aims to increase the contribution of the digital economy from approximately QR7bn in 2025 to QR11.6bn, while growing the digital sector’s contribution and improving Qatar’s access to major international markets.

The ministry’s representatives argued that digital exports could create a multiplier effect across the economy. As domestic companies develop products and services for international customers, they are likely to increase their investment in technology, strengthen their digital capabilities and generate further demand for ICT services.

This creates what ministry officials described as a digital export flywheel, in which successful international expansion drives further innovation, investment and growth across the technology sector.

The opportunity covers two broad areas: digitally delivered services, including cloud computing, artificial intelligence, fintech and digital content; and digitally ordered products sold through online platforms. However, Qatar still has considerable ground to cover before it can fully capitalise on this opportunity.

According to figures presented by MCIT, Qatar’s digitally delivered services market was valued at approximately QR4.3bn in 2023, representing around 0.56% of the global market. The country’s share of digitally ordered products was also relatively small.

More broadly, digital imports remain approximately 2.2 times higher than digital exports, highlighting the gap between domestic demand for technology and the ability of Qatari companies to compete internationally.

The comparison with other markets illustrates the scale of the opportunity. Ministry officials highlighted Singapore, where digital exports account for approximately 36% of the relevant economic activity, compared with around 9% in both the UAE and France, and approximately 2% in Qatar.

Closing that gap will require more than investment in infrastructure. It will mean helping domestic companies develop export-ready products, connecting them with international buyers, improving cross-border payment and delivery systems, and reducing the operational barriers associated with entering foreign markets.

Qatar has already established support mechanisms, including its Qatar Digital Export Support Programme and the Scale Now initiative, which aims to mentor, advise and connect local businesses with regional and international opportunities.

The ministry highlighted that 225 startups already have international exposure, while Qatar’s export support ecosystem has assisted more than 400 exporters and delivered 178 workshops and training sessions.

Nevertheless, officials identified several challenges, including uneven business maturity, limited access to foreign markets, high cross-border operating costs and difficulties in scaling products beyond Qatar.

Government investment at the heart of Qatar’s AI ambitions

Artificial intelligence (AI) is another important component of Qatar’s ambitions to become a global technology hub, with the government taking a central role in establishing the infrastructure and conditions required to accelerate adoption.

Speaking during the MWC26 Doha discussion, H.E. Reem Mohammed Al Mansoori, assistant undersecretary for digital industry affairs at MCIT, outlined how Qatar is approaching AI as a national transformation programme rather than a conventional technology deployment.

She described the speed of AI development as a significant challenge for government organisations, explaining that technologies that were still being considered during programme planning 18 months earlier had since become readily available.

“It developed so quickly, so fast. So what we were thinking 18 months back, today it becomes available, easy to implement,” she said.

This pace of change has required Qatar to adopt a more agile approach to government technology programmes, including working closely with international technology companies and implementation partners.

Al Mansoori argued that governments cannot leave AI infrastructure investment entirely to the private sector, given the scale of the resources required and the importance of making these capabilities accessible across the wider economy.

“With AI, the ecosystem cannot be replicated as previous technology has been growing and organically developed. With AI, everyone needs to work closely. The government needs to be at the heart of that,” she added.

She highlighted the importance of investing in datacentres, computing capacity, graphics processing units (GPUs) and shared services to enable organisations to develop and deploy AI applications without shouldering the full cost of the underlying infrastructure.

In Qatar, initiatives involving AI infrastructure, GPU capacity and shared digital services are intended to provide a common foundation on which government entities and private sector organisations can build their own use cases.

This approach reflects a broader ambition to make Qatar an attractive destination for AI development, enterprise innovation and technology investment.

However, Al Mansoori stressed that infrastructure alone would not guarantee successful AI adoption. Organisations must understand how AI can fundamentally change their operations, rather than simply using it to automate existing processes or reduce costs.

“You cannot just replicate any system with AI. You cannot just try to make any job effective just by using AI,” she said.

Instead, she argued that AI initiatives must be led by organisational leadership, supported by clear business objectives, and accompanied by change management and workforce reskilling.

Al Mansoori highlighted executive training programmes introduced in Qatar to help business and government leaders understand how AI could transform their organisations. The programmes have also evolved to encourage participants to bring forward real business use cases and develop plans for implementing them.

She emphasised that leadership readiness is critical to successful AI adoption, with employees at every level needing to understand how the technology will change their roles and the way organisations operate.

Connectivity and regional cooperation

Qatar’s digital ambitions are developing alongside a wider transformation of the telecommunications sector across MENA, where investment in next-generation networks is expected to support new industries, services and business models.

The GSMA forecasts that 5G connections will increase from 9% of the region’s total mobile connections in 2025 to 40% by 2030. Mobile operators are expected to invest $88.9bn over the same period.

Yet the region continues to face a significant connectivity challenge. Although 48% of the MENA population used mobile internet in 2025, a further 49% remained offline despite living in areas covered by mobile broadband networks.

This usage gap highlights the need to focus not only on network deployment, but also on affordability, digital skills, relevant services and the ability of businesses and citizens to benefit from connectivity.

At MWC26 Doha, GSMA director general Vivek Badrinath emphasised the importance of maintaining global industry standards and extending connectivity to underserved populations. “Progress only counts if everyone shares in it,” he said, highlighting the need for standards that ensure networks, services and devices remain interoperable across borders.

The next phase of Qatar’s digital transformation will therefore depend on its ability to connect infrastructure investment with commercial opportunities.

Building datacentres, expanding AI capabilities and improving connectivity will establish the foundations. But turning those investments into internationally competitive businesses will require stronger export capabilities, access to global markets, skilled talent and a supportive regulatory environment.
